title: BUG: Series.dt.to_pydatetime() returns a Series with a reset RangeIndex instead of preserving the parent index
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series(pd.to_datetime(["2026-01-01", "2026-02-01", "2026-03-01"]), index=[10, 11, 12])

print(s.dt.to_pydatetime().index)  # RangeIndex(start=0, stop=3, step=1)
print(s.dt.date.index)             # Index([10, 11, 12], dtype='int64')
print(s.dt.normalize().index)      # Index([10, 11, 12], dtype='int64')

 practical consequence is silent misalignment whenever the result is combined
with anything carrying the original index — for example a `groupby` slice, whose
index does not start at zero for any group after the first:

import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "g": ["a", "a", "b", "b"],
    "ts": pd.to_datetime(["2026-01-01", "2026-01-02", "2026-01-03", "2026-01-04"]),
    "x": [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0],
})

for key, sub in df.groupby("g"):
    out = pd.DataFrame({"ts": sub["ts"].dt.to_pydatetime(), "x": sub["x"]})
    print(key, len(sub), "->", len(out))


Output:


a 2 -> 2
b 2 -> 4


Group `b` is silently doubled and half-NaN:


                    ts    x
0  2026-01-03 00:00:00  NaN
1  2026-01-04 00:00:00  NaN
2                  NaN  3.0
3                  NaN  4.0
```

### Issue Description

`Series.dt.to_pydatetime()` changed from returning an `ndarray` (pandas 2.x) to
returning a `Series` (pandas 3.0). That return-type change was deprecated ahead
of time and is not what this report is about.

The problem is that the new `Series` is built without the parent index:

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/pandas/core/indexes/accessors.py

```python
def to_pydatetime(self) -> Series:
    # GH#20306
    from pandas import Series

    return Series(self._get_values().to_pydatetime(), dtype=object)
```

There is no `index=self._parent.index`, so the result always comes back on a
fresh `RangeIndex`. Every other `.dt` accessor result preserves the index, which
makes this an inconsistency rather than a deliberate choice as far as I can tell.

It fails silently: no exception and no warning. Code that used to get an
index-free `ndarray` under 2.x, and therefore aligned positionally, now aligns on
a `RangeIndex` that happens to be wrong. Where the original index is contiguous
from 0 the results still agree, so the breakage is invisible in the common case
and appears only on reindexed or grouped data.

Two smaller points in the same area:

1. The docstring's `Returns` section still reads `numpy.ndarray` /
   "Object dtype array containing native Python datetime objects", which no
   longer matches the annotated `-> Series` return type.
2. `ArrowTemporalProperties.to_pydatetime()` takes a different path
   (`ArrowExtensionArray._dt_to_pydatetime()`), so it is worth confirming the two
   accessors agree on index handling once this is fixed.

### Expected Behavior

`s.dt.to_pydatetime()` should return a `Series` carrying `s`'s index, consistent
with `s.dt.date`, `s.dt.normalize()`, and the other `.dt` accessors:

```
Series(self._get_values().to_pydatetime(), index=self._parent.index, dtype=object)
```

```python
    @contextmanager
``` 

### Reproducible Example

```python
>>> import pandas as pd
>>> s = pd.Series([1, float('nan'), None, 4])
>>> with pd.option_context('styler.format.na_rep', '--'):
...     print(s)
...

2    NaN
3    4.0
dtype: float64
```

### Issue Description

`"styler.format.na_rep"` option is not respected inside `pd.option_context()` context. Same behavior regardless if `dtype=object` or `float`.

Note that this is not a duplicate of https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/54872, becaue `.to_string()` method seems to work fine:
```py
>>> print(s.to_string(na_rep='--'))
0    1.0
1     --
2     --
3    4.0
```

### Expected Behavior

Expected output:
```     
0    1.0
1     --
2     --
3    4.0
dtype: float64
```

pandas                : 3.0.3

title: ENH: UnicodeDecodeError from read_csv could suggest common alternative encodings
body:
### Feature Type

- [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

I wish read_csv's UnicodeDecodeError gave me a hint about what to try next, instead of just failing with no direction.

When read_csv hits a UnicodeDecodeError (e.g. a Windows Excel export saved as cp1252), the error gives no indication that trying a different encoding is the likely fix.

Reproducible example (pandas 3.0.2):

with open('test.csv', 'wb') as f:
    f.write(b'name,note\n')
    f.write(b'test,em' + bytes([0x97]) + b'dash\n')  # valid cp1252, invalid utf-8

import pandas as pd
pd.read_csv('test.csv')

Result:
UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0x97 in position 17: invalid start byte

This is a very common situation, Windows Excel commonly exports CSVs as cp1252, not utf-8, and the fix is almost always trying encoding='latin-1' or encoding='cp1252'. But nothing in the error message points there, so new users often don't realize encoding is even the problem.

### Feature Description

Append a short hint to the UnicodeDecodeError raised during CSV parsing when the default utf-8 encoding fails and the user hasn't explicitly set encoding.

Rough approach, in the CSV reading error handling path:

try:
    ...read with utf-8...
except UnicodeDecodeError as e:
    if encoding_was_default:
        raise UnicodeDecodeError(
            e.encoding, e.object, e.start, e.end,
            e.reason + ". Tip: this file may not be UTF-8 encoded. "
            "Try encoding='latin-1' or encoding='cp1252', common with Windows Excel exports."
        ) from e
    raise

This only changes the message text, not behavior, and only fires when encoding wasn't explicitly passed by the user, so it doesn't affect anyone who already specifies an encoding.

### Alternative Solutions

Currently the only options are:

1. Manually try common encodings one by one (utf-8, latin-1, cp1252) until one works, usually after searching Stack Overflow to learn this is the fix
2. Use a third-party library like chardet or charset-normalizer to detect the encoding beforehand, which is a heavier dependency for a one-line hint
3. Open the file in a text editor that reports encoding, then pass it explicitly

None of these are discoverable from the error message itself, which is the actual gap this request addresses.

### Additional Context

This is intentionally scoped narrower than a full encoding='detect' feature, since I understand that's a bigger design discussion. This is just improving the existing error message text for the common case.

title: BUG: ArrowDtype timestamp comparison with datetime.date scalar loses null propagation
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
import datetime

ts = pd.Series(
    [pd.Timestamp("2024-01-01"), None, pd.Timestamp("2024-06-15")],
    dtype="timestamp[ns][pyarrow]",
)

# Cross-type comparison: timestamp vs datetime.date
result_eq = ts == datetime.date(2024, 1, 1)
print(result_eq)
# 0    False   ← should be True (values are equal)
# 1    False   ← should be <NA> (null propagation)
# 2    False
# dtype: bool[pyarrow]

# Same-type comparison works correctly
result_same = ts == pd.Timestamp("2024-01-01")
print(result_same)
# 0     True
# 1     <NA>
# 2    False
# dtype: bool[pyarrow]
```

### Issue Description

When comparing a Series with ArrowDtype timestamp type against a `datetime.date` scalar (or `date32[day][pyarrow]` Series), pandas falls back to object-level comparison instead of delegating to pyarrow's `pc.equal()`. This causes two problems:

1. **Null values return `False` instead of `<NA>`** — null propagation is lost
2. **Equal values return `False`** — because at the Python object level, `Timestamp("2024-01-01") == datetime.date(2024, 1, 1)` evaluates to `False`

The same issue affects `!=` (`ne`), where nulls return `True` instead of `<NA>`.

pyarrow handles this correctly natively:

```python
import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.compute as pc

arr = pa.array([pd.Timestamp("2024-01-01"), None, pd.Timestamp("2024-06-15")], type=pa.timestamp("ns"))
scalar = pa.scalar(datetime.date(2024, 1, 1), type=pa.date32())
print(pc.equal(arr, scalar))  # [true, null, false]
```

### Expected Behavior

pandas should cast `datetime.date` to the Series' timestamp type (or delegate to `pc.equal()` which handles cross-type timestamp/date32 comparison natively) and propagate nulls:

```
0     True
1     <NA>
2    False
dtype: bool[pyarrow]
```

### Installed Versions

Tested and reproduced on:

- pandas 3.0.3 + pyarrow 23.0.1
- pandas 3.0.3 + pyarrow 25.0.0
- pandas main (3.1.0.dev0+1362.g54d39de0d9) + pyarrow 25.0.0

title: ENH: Support `tz_convert` on naive timestamps when naive tz specified
body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

It is quite common to defensively convert-or-assume timestamps to UTC, which means writing something like this:

```python
def my_function(df: pd.Dataframe, time: pd.Timestamp) -> pd.Dataframe:
    if time.tzinfo is None:
        time = time.tz_localize("UTC")
    else:
        time = time.tz_convert("UTC")
    ...
    return df.assign(time=time)
```

Alternatively an inline if can be used

```python
time = time.tz_localize("UTC") if time.tz is None else time.tz_convert("UTC")
```

But this is slightly longwinded, so often helper functions are repeated in loads of modules

```python
def _ensure_utc(time: pd.Timestamp) -> pd.Timestamp:
    return (
        time.tz_localize("UTC")
        if time.tz is None
        else time.tz_convert("UTC")
    )
```

My opinion is that neither the rather long if..else expression nor the usually-not-consistently-named helper method are very readable. There can also be challenges around proper typing on the helper method, when support for e.g. series and datetime index is required as well. This feature request is essentially asking for a shorthand that is native to Pandas for this pattern.

### Feature Description

Add a keyword argument to `tz_convert` which specifies how naive timestamps should be interpreted, instead of raising an error:


```python
time = time.tz_convert("UTC", naive_tz="UTC")
```

It would be functionally equivalent to `time.tz_localize("UTC") if time.tz is None else time.tz_convert("UTC")` - just a shorthand. Of course, `tz_convert` on series, datetime index etc should have the same support.

### Alternative Solutions

"Keeping the status quo" is more verbose and works. The feature request is mainly to make the convert-or-assume pattern easier to both write and read.

But some alternatives that go along the same lines:

- Different keyword arg names, e.g. `.tz_convert("UTC", assume_naive="UTC")`
    - Particularly, putting the verb "assume" might be good for clarity of what the arg does. It's just longer so I didn't put it in the main suggestion (I think the main suggestion is clear enough).
- "Policy style" instead of specific tz, `.tz_convert("UTC", naive="assume_utc")`, `.tz_convert("UTC", naive="assume_local")`
    - This could have a default of `naive="raise"` which neatly describes the current behaviour correctly while keeping `tz=None` semantics constant. However it obviously loses the ability to set an arbitrary naive timezone to use. 
- Different specific method, e.g. `.tz_ensure("UTC", assume="UTC")`
    - If someone thinks we're changing the semantics of `tz_convert` too hard. I don't think so, but had to be mentioned.

### Additional Context

_No response_

title: BUG: read_csv(dtype="category") ignores dtype_backend for the c and python engines
body:
### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO

data = "a,b\n1,2\n3,4\n"

df = pd.read_csv(
    StringIO(data), dtype={"a": "category"}, dtype_backend="numpy_nullable"
)
df.dtypes
# a    category
# b       Int64

df["a"].cat.categories.dtype
# dtype('int64')   <- numpy, but `b` in the same frame is Int64
```

### Issue Description

Since GH-56044, `read_csv` with `dtype="category"` infers numeric and boolean categories instead of leaving them as strings. That inference does not consult `dtype_backend`, so the c and python engines produce numpy-dtyped categories even when every other column in the same frame gets a nullable or arrow dtype.

Category element dtype for `"a\n1\n2"`, against what the same column gets *without* `dtype="category"`:

| engine | `numpy_nullable` | `pyarrow` |
|---|---|---|
| c | `int64` (non-cat: `Int64`) | `int64` (non-cat: `int64[pyarrow]`) |
| python | `int64` (non-cat: `Int64`) | `int64[pyarrow]` :heavy_check_mark: |
| pyarrow | `Int64` :heavy_check_mark: | `int64[pyarrow]` :heavy_check_mark: |

Three of six combinations disagree with the non-categorical result. The current behavior is pinned by `test_categorical_dtype_non_default_dtype_backend`.

Two notes on why the passing cells already work, since they're inconsistent for different reasons:

- The **pyarrow engine** is correct only incidentally: `_post_convert_dtypes` in `pandas/io/_util.py` is gated on `dtype_backend is lib.no_default or dtype_backend == "numpy"`, so an explicit backend skips the `IntegerDtype`->numpy downcast that would otherwise apply.
- The **python engine + `pyarrow`** case works because its values arrive as arrow-backed strings and `to_numeric` returns `int64[pyarrow]` directly -- not because the backend was consulted.

So neither reflects a deliberate path, and a fix should converge all three engines rather than extend either mechanism.

### Expected Behavior

Categories should honor `dtype_backend` the same way ordinary columns do -- `Int64` under `numpy_nullable`, `int64[pyarrow]` under `pyarrow`, numpy `int64` under the default.

This likely means threading `dtype_backend` through `Categorical._from_inferred_categories` and both the C and python parser call sites, and reconciling the pyarrow engine's separate `_post_convert_dtypes` route so the three engines share one rule.

title: BUG: `str.split()`/`rsplit()` with no separator on `ArrowDtype` keeps empty whitespace tokens
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
import pyarrow as pa

s = pd.Series(["  hi  there ", ""], dtype=pd.ArrowDtype(pa.string()))
print(s.str.split().tolist())
```

### Issue Description

Calling `.str.split()` with no separator on an `ArrowDtype` string column returns extra empty strings when values have leading or trailing whitespace (and [''] instead of [] for empty strings), unlike Python's `str.split()` or the other pandas backends. It happens because the Arrow implementation calls pyarrow's `utf8_split_whitespace` directly, which doesn't drop those empty pieces the way `str.split()` does.

### Expected Behavior

`.str.split()` with no separator should match Python's `str.split()`, giving `[['hi', 'there'], []]`

title: BUG: Segfaults from various python api call return values not being checked during encode by ujson
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas._libs._ujson as ujson
ujson.ujson_dumps({1 << 1_000_000: "value"})

LONE_SURROGATE = "\ud800"

class InvalidDecimal(decimal.Decimal):
    def __format__(self, *a, **kw):
        return LONE_SURROGATE
ujson.ujson_dumps(InvalidDecimal(1))
```

### Issue Description

There are three python api call patterns that ujson objToJson doesn't reliably check the result code for:
 - Converting unicode to utf8. (for example "\ud800" can fail)
 - Converting very large integers to string
 - Calling Various dunder methods that usually behave predicably.

I came into this via some fuzz testing I was doing, which found this:

```
ujson.ujson_dumps({1 << 1_000_000: "value"})
```

But then a review of the `objToJSON` with the help of codex came up with the following inputs that cause ujson to segfault:
 - [X] decimal.Decimal subclasses with a `__format__` method that returns a lone surrogate [#66357]
 - [X] `datetime.time` subclasses whose `isoformat()` return a non-string, or lone surrogate value [#66357]
 - [ ] `__dir__` methods on objects that raise
 - [ ] `__dir__` methods on objects that return a lone surrogate value.
 - [ ] Set() subclasses whose `__iter__` raises
 - [X] encoding int values whose string representation > `sys.get_int_max_str_digits()` digits long [#66357]
 - [ ] `dict` keys that are lone surrogate values
 - [ ] `dict` keys that are `int` values that are too long
 - [ ] `dict` keys that are are objects whose `__str__()` method returns a lone surrogate.
 - [ ] 'labels' arrays with invalid surrogate values

All of these are unusual/obscure cases, and apart from the massive int case, are not exercisable just by processing 'untrusted' data.

The fixes here are just to check the respective python api calls and handle them appropriately.

<details>
<summary>Unit tests</summary>

```
LONE_SURROGATE = "\ud800"

def test_encode_invalid_decimal_subclass(self):
    class InvalidDecimal(decimal.Decimal):
        def __format__(self, *a, **kw):
            return LONE_SURROGATE

    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="surrogates not allowed"):
        ujson.ujson_dumps(InvalidDecimal(1))

def test_encode_dict_with_lone_surrogate_key(self):
    lone_surrogate_dict = {LONE_SURROGATE: "value1"}
    with pytest.raises(UnicodeEncodeError, match="surrogates not allowed"):
        ujson.ujson_dumps(lone_surrogate_dict)

def test_encode_time_invalid_subclass_surrogate(self):
    class InvalidTime(datetime.time):
        def isoformat(self):
            return LONE_SURROGATE

    with pytest.raises(UnicodeEncodeError, match="surrogates not allowed"):
        ujson.ujson_dumps(InvalidTime())

def test_encode_time_invalid_subclass_non_str(self):
    class InvalidTime(datetime.time):
        def isoformat(self):
            return 1

    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="Failed to convert time"):
        ujson.ujson_dumps(InvalidTime())

def test_encode_object_bad_dir(self):
    class _TestObj:
        def __dir__(self):
            raise TypeError("I raise you one exception")

    obj = _TestObj()
    with pytest.raises(TypeError, match="I raise you one exception"):
        ujson.ujson_dumps(obj)

def test_encode_object_dir_surrogate(self):
    class _TestObj:
        def __dir__(self):
            return [LONE_SURROGATE]

    obj = _TestObj()
    with pytest.raises(UnicodeEncodeError, match="surrogates not allowed"):
        ujson.ujson_dumps(obj)

def test_encode_bad_set(self):
    class MySet(set):
        def __iter__(self):
            raise TypeError("I raise you one exception")

    with pytest.raises(TypeError, match="I raise you one exception"):
        ujson.ujson_dumps(MySet([1, 2, 3]))

def test_encode_large_int_object(self):
    cur_limit = sys.get_int_max_str_digits()
    sys.set_int_max_str_digits(1000)
    try:
        with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="Exceeds the limit"):
            ujson.ujson_dumps(1 << 1_000_000)
    finally:
        sys.set_int_max_str_digits(cur_limit)

def test_encode_large_int_object_key(self):
    cur_limit = sys.get_int_max_str_digits()
    sys.set_int_max_str_digits(1000)
    try:
        with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="Exceeds the limit"):
            ujson.ujson_dumps({1 << 1_000_000: "value"})
    finally:
        sys.set_int_max_str_digits(cur_limit)

def test_encode_labels_invalid_str(self):
    class LoneSurrogateProxy:
        def __str__(self):
            return LONE_SURROGATE

    df = DataFrame({LoneSurrogateProxy(): [1, 2, 3]})
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="surrogates not allowed"):
        ujson.ujson_dumps(df)
```

</details>

No crashes/segfaults.

title: DOC: Series.eq() fill_value docs outdated for string dtype
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that the issue still exists on the latest versions of the docs on `main` [here](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/)


### Location of the documentation

https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.eq


## Problem

The docs for `Series.eq()` specify that `fill_value` accepts `float | None` only.
However, passing a string `fill_value` works correctly at runtime when the Series has `dtype='string'`.

## Reproducible Example

import pandas as pd

s1 = pd.Series(["a", "b", None], dtype="string")
s2 = pd.Series(["a", "c", "d"], dtype="string")

result = s1.eq(s2, fill_value="missing")
print(result)

## Output
0     True
1    False
2    False
dtype: boolean

## Expected behavior

Docs should reflect that `fill_value` accepts a string value when 
dtype is `'string'`.

## Note

Originally raised by @geoffrey-eisenbarth in pandas-stubs#1797.

### Suggested fix for documentation

Update the `fill_value` parameter description in `Series.eq()` docs from:

> fill_value : float or None, default None

To:

> fill_value : float, str, or None, default None

title: REF: Reduce cognitive complexity of `tokenize_bytes`
body:
The [`tokenize_bytes`](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/15b1dd913e3df72854955936b0d89c7f95648a9a/pandas/_libs/src/parser/tokenizer.c#L779-L1357) function currently has a cognitive complexity score of 551 according to `clang-tidy`, which significantly exceeds the default threshold of 25.

The complexity primarily comes from managing 16 distinct parser states within a single monolithic loop, combined with inline SIMD preprocessing and scalar fallback logic. Modularizing the state handling into smaller helper functions would help improve the readability and long-term maintainability of the CSV parser.

title: DEPR: `groupby.nth.__getitem__`
body:
The `nth` method on groupby can be called in 2 ways

```python
df.groupby(...).nth([0, 1])
df.groupby(...).nth[0, 1]
```

Which both dispatch to the same implementation

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/633e72f17a6e94dd1d350320ab10caf0c25d5300/pandas/core/groupby/indexing.py#L371-L379

In the original issue it was stated the `__getitem__` route is just syntactic sugar, https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/44589.

IMO it would be clearer and simpler if there was one form to call this API, and since `dropna` is an argument, the `__getitem__` implementation should be deprecated

title: BUG: False ChainedAssignmentError, misattributed to the caller, when setitem runs in Cython-compiled code — and no supported way to disable the check
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example


Two files. `repro_mod.py` contains only a plain, legal column assignment on
a function-local DataFrame — no mask, no intermediate object, no second
subscript:

```python
# repro_mod.py
import pandas as pd


def legal_assignment():
    df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3]})
    df["b"] = df["a"] * 2
    return df

```
```python
# run_repro.py
import warnings

import pandas as pd

import repro_mod

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    df = repro_mod.legal_assignment()

assert df["b"].tolist() == [2, 4, 6]  # the assignment itself worked fine

chained = [w for w in caught
           if issubclass(w.category, pd.errors.ChainedAssignmentError)]

if not chained:
    print("OK: no warning")
else:
    for w in chained:
        print(f"FALSE POSITIVE: {w.category.__name__} "
              f"attributed to {w.filename}:{w.lineno}")
```

Run it twice — once with the module as plain Python, once after compiling
that same module into a C extension with Cython:

```shell
$ python run_repro.py
```
OK: no warning

```shell
$ cythonize -3 -i repro_mod.py
$ python run_repro.py
```
FALSE POSITIVE: ChainedAssignmentError attributed to ...\run_repro.py:10


Identical source, identical runner. Note the attribution: `run_repro.py:10`
is `df = repro_mod.legal_assignment()` — the *caller*, which performs no
assignment at all. In a larger application this misattribution points at
whatever pure-Python frame happens to sit below the compiled code (in ours,
the application's `MainLoop()` call in the entry module), which makes the
warning extremely hard to trace back to its real origin.

### Issue Description

`DataFrame.__setitem__` (pandas 3.0.3, `pandas/core/frame.py:4642`; the same
pattern guards every `ChainedAssignmentError` site in `frame.py`,
`series.py`, `generic.py`, and `indexing.py`) detects chained assignment
with two heuristics:

```python
if not CHAINED_WARNING_DISABLED:
    if sys.getrefcount(self) <= REF_COUNT and not com.is_local_in_caller_frame(self):
        warnings.warn(_chained_assignment_msg, ChainedAssignmentError, stacklevel=2)
```

Both heuristics assume the caller is interpreted CPython code, and both
misfire when the caller is a compiled extension:

1. **Refcount** — a Cython function keeps `df` in a C variable rather than
   in a frame's locals, so `sys.getrefcount(df)` inside `__setitem__` sits
   at the temporary-object level even though `df` is a genuine local.
2. **Frame inspection** — `is_local_in_caller_frame`
   (`pandas/core/common.py:662`) looks for the object in
   `sys._getframe(2).f_locals`. Cython functions do not create Python frame
   objects, so `sys._getframe(2)` skips past the real caller entirely and
   lands on an unrelated pure-Python frame further down the stack. The
   rescue check fails, and `stacklevel=2` attributes the warning to that
   unrelated frame.

The same failure mode applies to any frame-less caller (Cython, mypyc, and
similar ahead-of-time compilers).

Filtering the warning is not a real workaround: with
`warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=ChainedAssignmentError)` the
message disappears but the detection machinery still runs. Because the
refcount test always passes for compiled callers, **every** setitem from
compiled code takes the slow path — `sys._getframe(2)`, a full `f_locals`
materialisation, and the `warnings` machinery. We measured roughly 4 µs per
assignment on small frames (Python 3.11, Windows) — a permanent tax on
exactly the code that was compiled for speed.

A short-circuit for this already exists: `CHAINED_WARNING_DISABLED`
(`pandas/compat/_constants.py`) skips the whole block, including both
heuristics. But it is a constant computed from the interpreter type
(`= PYPY`) — informational only, with no supported way for an application
to set it.

Suggested fix — either or both:

- Provide a supported opt-out that feeds `CHAINED_WARNING_DISABLED`, e.g.
  an environment variable (`PANDAS_CHAINED_WARNING_DISABLED=1`), mirroring
  how `PANDAS_COPY_ON_WRITE` was handled during the CoW rollout.
- Suppress the warning when frame inspection cannot positively identify the
  caller (i.e. when the frame walk cannot see the object at all): a
  heuristic that cannot observe its evidence should not fire.

### Expected Behavior

A plain `df["b"] = ...` on a function-local DataFrame should not raise
`ChainedAssignmentError` regardless of whether the enclosing function is
interpreted or compiled — and applications embedding pandas in compiled
code should have a supported way to opt out of the detection overhead
entirely.

### Reproducible Example

### Problem Description
Concatenating many small DataFrames with homogeneous (often identical) columns or index `RangeIndex` objects spends significant time in `union_indexes` and `RangeIndex.union`. 

For example, when concatenating 2,000 small DataFrames along `axis=0` with identical columns, `union_indexes` is called on a list of 2,000 `RangeIndex(0, 10)` objects. Currently, this performs a loop of 1,999 sequential `result.union(other)` calls, which incurs high type check, name reconciliation (`_get_reconciled_name_object`), and new index object creation overhead (consuming over 50% of the runtime).

### Reproducible Example
```python
import pandas as pd
import time

# 2,000 small DataFrames with identical columns
dfs = [pd.DataFrame(0, index=[i], columns=pd.RangeIndex(0, 10)) for i in range(2000)]

t0 = time.perf_counter()
pd.concat(dfs)
t1 = time.perf_counter()
print(f"Concatenation time: {t1 - t0:.4f} seconds")
```

### Proposed Solution
Add a fast-path inside `union_indexes` when all input indices are `RangeIndex` instances:

- Deduplicate them quickly using a set of (range, name) tuples.
- If all unique non-empty indices share the same step and name, check if they are contiguous/overlapping (no gaps).
- If they are contiguous, directly return a single `RangeIndex` spanning the start/stop range.
- Otherwise, fall back to the standard union logic but only iterate over the deduplicated unique `RangeIndexes`.

title: BUG: merge_asof says "tolerance must be positive" but accepts tolerance=0
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the main branch of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

left = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 5, 10], "left_val": ["a", "b", "c"]})
right = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 6, 10], "right_val": ["A", "B", "C"]})

# tolerance=0 is accepted and meaningful: exact-match-only
print(pd.merge_asof(left, right, on="a", tolerance=0))
#     a left_val right_val
# 0   1        a         A
# 1   5        b       NaN   <- no exact match within 0
# 2  10        c         C

# but a negative tolerance is rejected with a message that claims 0 is invalid too:
pd.merge_asof(left, right, on="a", tolerance=-1)
# MergeError: tolerance must be positive
```

### Issue Description

`merge_asof` accepts `tolerance=0` (which means exact-match-only, a meaningful asof semantic), but the error raised for an invalid `tolerance` says it `must be positive`. The three guards in `_MergeOperation`/`_AsOfMerge` reject only strictly-negative values:

```python
if self.tolerance < Timedelta(0):
    raise MergeError("tolerance must be positive")
...
if self.tolerance < 0:
    raise MergeError("tolerance must be positive")
```

So `0` is accepted, yet "must be positive" (which means `> 0`) excludes it. The message is inconsistent with the guard.

### Expected Behavior

The message should say `tolerance must be non-negative`, matching the values the guard actually accepts.

### Installed Versions

<details>

Reproduced on `main` and pandas 3.0.3.

</details>

title: BUG: MultiIndex.set_levels/set_codes give self-contradictory "must be list-like" error for a nested value with a scalar level
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the main branch of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

mi = pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples([("a", 1), ("b", 2)], names=["l", "n"])
mi.set_levels([["x", "y"]], level=0)
```

### Issue Description

`MultiIndex.set_levels` (and `set_codes`) raise a self-contradictory message when a **single, scalar** `level` is paired with a **nested** (list-of-lists) value:

```
TypeError: Levels must be list-like
```

The value `[["x", "y"]]` *is* list-like — that's precisely why control reaches this branch. In `_require_listlike` (`pandas/core/indexes/multi.py`), the scalar-level branch first rejects a non-list-like `arr` with `"must be list-like"`, and then rejects a *nested* `arr` (a list of lists) with the **same** string, which is a copy-paste of the first message:

```python
if level is not None and not is_list_like(level):
    if not is_list_like(arr):
        raise TypeError(f"{arrname} must be list-like")          # arr is not list-like — message correct
    if len(arr) > 0 and is_list_like(arr[0]):
        raise TypeError(f"{arrname} must be list-like")          # arr IS list-like (nested) — message wrong
```

For a scalar level the value must be a *flat* list-like, so the second message should say that, not repeat "must be list-like".

### Expected Behavior

The nested-value case should raise a message that names the real constraint, e.g.:

```
TypeError: Levels must be list-like, not a list of lists-like
```

which mirrors the existing `"must be list of lists-like"` message used for the list-valued `level` branch.

### Installed Versions

<details>

main branch (`_require_listlike` in `pandas/core/indexes/multi.py`).

</details>

title: ENH: Optimize Series.apply User-Defined Functions (UDFs) via JIT Compilation Engine Option
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

### Problem Description
Invoking `.apply()` with custom Python functions is notoriously slow in Pandas because it loops over rows in pure Python (the "UDF bottleneck"). For large Series, this element-by-element interpreter call pattern adds massive overhead.

While Pandas supports Numba engines in GroupBy and Rolling window methods, standard `.apply()` lacks direct JIT compilation engines to accelerate simple mathematical/branching row-level functions.

### Proposed Feature
Introduce a JIT compilation execution engine option inside `Series.apply()`.
1. **Explicit Opt-in**: Support `engine="numba"` and `engine_kwargs` parameters in `Series.apply()`. If specified, JIT compile the UDF using Numba and execute via a fast parallelized JIT loop dispatcher.
2. **Global Configuration Option**: Support automatic transparent JIT execution on large numeric/datetime Series ($\ge 50,000$ elements) if the global option `pd.set_option("compute.use_numba", True)` is enabled.
3. **Correctness & Error Boundaries**: 
   - When explicitly opted-in (`engine="numba"`), raise a `NumbaUtilError` or `ValueError` if compilation or input dtype constraints fail.
   - When implicitly run via the global configuration, fall back silently to the Python interpreter on any compilation warnings/errors to maintain 100% backward-compatibility.

### Code Example / Benchmark Comparison
For a UDF with branching math operations over a Series of 1,000,000 floats:
```python
def my_func(x):
    if x > 0:
        return math.sin(x) * math.exp(-x)
    else:
        return math.cos(x) * 1.5
```
### Standard apply: ~870ms
### JIT apply (engine="numba", cached): ~37ms  (~23.4x speedup)

title: PERF: Fast-path DataFrame.dropna for homogeneous single-block DataFrames
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

**Description:**

### Problem Description
Currently, calling `DataFrame.dropna()` on a homogeneous single-block DataFrame (e.g. a float64 or object DataFrame) goes through the general multi-block BlockManager reconciliation and `.loc` index slicing path.
This involves:
1. Allocating a temporary boolean DataFrame (`notna_obj`) to check null entries.
2. Allocating a temporary boolean Series (`mask`) during reduction along `axis=1`.
3. Invoking `.loc[mask]`, which checks label alignment and calls `BlockManager.reindex_indexer()`.

For medium or wide homogeneous DataFrames, these temporary object allocations and BlockManager layout validations are the primary bottleneck.

### Proposed Optimization
Introduce a fast path in `DataFrame.dropna` when there is no `subset`/`thresh` requested and `len(self._mgr.blocks) == 1`.
- If the block cannot hold NaNs (e.g., integer/boolean), we immediately return a copy (or inplace-update the index if `ignore_index=True`), running in $O(1)$ time.
- Perform direct vectorized C/NumPy NaN checks on the block values (e.g., `np.isnan(values)`).
- Package the sliced boolean values directly into a single `Block` and wrap it in a `BlockManager` via `new_block_2d` and `BlockManager`, completely bypassing `.loc` indexing and metadata-heavy reindexing paths.

### Performance Impact
Significant latency reduction on common smaller/medium datasets and wide homogeneous tables.

title: DEPR: Using lists and tuples interchangeably in resample
body:
Ref: https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/65807#discussion_r3383822680

```python
dti = pd.date_range(start=datetime(2005, 1, 1), end=datetime(2005, 1, 10), freq="Min")
test_series = pd.Series(np.random.default_rng(2).random(len(dti)), dti)
test_frame = pd.DataFrame({"A": test_series, "B": test_series, "C": np.arange(len(dti))})
r = test_frame.resample("h")["A", "B"]
```

The value passed to `__getitem__` on the last line here is `("A", "B")`, which is currently being treated the same way a list would in

    r = test_frame.resample("h")[["A", "B"]]

This should instead be treated as accessing a MultiIndex with levels `"A"` and `"B"` (which does not exist here, raising a KeyError instead).

title: PERF: Skip full array allocation in RangeIndex.isin for small query inputs
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

**Description:**

### Problem Description
Currently, calling `RangeIndex.isin(values)` delegates to the generic `Index.isin` implementation. This accesses `self._values`, which forces the RangeIndex to fully instantiate its entire integer range array in memory (e.g. allocating a contiguous 80MB NumPy array for a RangeIndex of size 10,000,000), followed by building a hash table or running `algos.isin` on the generated array.

If the search query `values` has only a small number of elements, this is highly inefficient.

### Proposed Optimization
Implement `RangeIndex.isin` directly. When `len(values) < len(self)`, we can allocate a boolean output array of size `len(self)` and mathematically check which query values are in the RangeIndex using CPython's $O(1)$ `range.__contains__` check.
If present, we set the corresponding boolean array location in $O(1)$ using the computed index:
`idx = (val - start) // step`

For large queries where `len(values) >= len(self)`, we delegate back to `super().isin(values)` to leverage C-level array hashing.

### Performance Impact
- Eliminates the memory allocation of the full RangeIndex integer array (80MB for a 10M range index).
- Speeds up membership checks by bypassing array generation and hash searches.

title: PERF: C-Import low-level Cython utilities to bypass Python dispatch overhead
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

**Description:**

### Problem Description
Currently, several internal pandas Cython modules use standard Python imports (e.g. `from pandas._libs.algos import ...`) to load other compiled internal functions instead of Cython `cimport` mechanisms.
Specifically, in `pandas/_libs/groupby.pyx` and `pandas/_libs/internals.pyx`, functions like `groupsort_indexer`, `take_2d_axis1_bool_bool`, `take_2d_axis1_float64_float64`, and `ensure_int64` are imported via standard Python imports.

This causes:
1. Python-level symbol lookup and dispatch overhead when these compiled routines are called.
2. Dynamic lookup through module dictionaries instead of direct C-level function calls.

### Proposed Optimization
By declaring these functions as `cpdef` in `algos.pxd` / `.pyx` and `cimporting` them directly in the consumer modules, Cython can generate direct C-level function calls, bypassing the Python symbol resolution wrapper.
Additionally, call sites can be updated to pass arguments positionally to ensure fast C-level execution.

### Performance Impact
Reduces function call overhead for low-level groupby indexers, array taking operations, and internals block alignment routines.

title: BUG: parallel read_csv (GH-64347) diverges from the serial path in several cases
body:
Adversarial testing of the parallel `read_csv` path added in GH-64347 turned up several cases where the parallel result diverges from the serial (`mode.max_threads=1`) result on the *same* file. Reporting them together since most share a root cause. All reproduce on `main` through the default path on a non-Windows machine (files must exceed the 50 MB parallel threshold).

### Root cause for most of these: the parallel path ignores `low_memory=False`

`_can_parallelize_csv` never consults `low_memory`, so `read_csv(big_file, low_memory=False)` is still split into `n_workers` byte-range chunks. That reintroduces exactly the per-chunk type/NA-inference divergences that `low_memory=False` exists to prevent: a "lean" chunk sees a different value distribution than the whole file and infers differently. Bug 2 and Bug 3 below are both instances of this.

---

### 🔴 Bug 1 — `EmptyDataError` on a valid headerless file with a blank first line

`header=None` (without `names`) on a file whose first physical line is blank or whitespace-only raises, where the serial path reads it fine (it skips the blank line).

```python
import os, pandas as pd

with open("f1.csv", "wb") as fh:
    fh.write(b"\n")  # leading blank line
    fh.write(b"".join(f"{i},{i*2},x{i}\n".encode() for i in range(2_600_000)))  # ~59 MB

pd.read_csv("f1.csv", header=None)
# -> EmptyDataError: No columns to parse from file

with pd.option_context("mode.max_threads", 1):
    pd.read_csv("f1.csv", header=None)   # OK, (2600000, 3)
```

**Cause:** in `_read_csv_parallel`, column-name inference builds `name_buf = preamble + first_line`; when `first_line` is blank, `TextFileReader(name_buf, ...)` raises `EmptyDataError`. That is not a `ParserError` subclass, so the `except (ParserError, UnicodeDecodeError)` fallback in `_read` doesn't catch it. Also fires when `skiprows` lands `data_start` on a blank line with `header=None`. (The `names=[...]` form falls back cleanly via the `n_first_rows != 1` guard — only bare `header=None` crashes.)

**Fix:** catch `EmptyDataError` around the name-inference `TextFileReader` and `return None` (fall back). Falling back is always safe: if the serial path would also raise, we reproduce it. Validated locally, 78 tests in `test_parallel_read.py` still pass.

---

### 🔴 Bug 2 — `dtype_backend="pyarrow"` raises on large ints where serial succeeds

A chunk that sees only large integers (> 2⁵³) attempts a numeric/pyarrow conversion and raises, while the whole-file serial read keeps the column as `double`/string.

```python
import pandas as pd

BIG = "9223372036854775807"
with open("f2.csv", "w") as fh:
    fh.write("c0\n")
    fh.write("\n".join("1.5" if i == 2_000_000 else BIG for i in range(4_000_000)))  # ~76 MB
    fh.write("\n")

pd.read_csv("f2.csv", dtype_backend="pyarrow", low_memory=False)
# -> pyarrow.lib.ArrowInvalid: Integer value 9223372036854775807 not in range ...

with pd.option_context("mode.max_threads", 1):
    pd.read_csv("f2.csv", dtype_backend="pyarrow", low_memory=False)   # OK, dtype double[pyarrow]
```

The guard treats `int`-kind + `float`-kind chunks as safe to `concat`, which holds for numpy/`numpy_nullable` but not pyarrow (its `concat` does a checked int→double cast that fails above 2⁵³). Depending on magnitude the parallel path raises `ArrowInvalid` (int in `[2⁵³, 2⁶⁴)`) or `OverflowError` (`> 2⁶⁴`). This is **pyarrow-specific** — `numpy` and `numpy_nullable` match serial in all cases tested. Note that with the default `low_memory=True`, a large file makes the serial path chunk internally too, so *both* raise; the clean parallel-only regression is under `low_memory=False`.

---

### 🔴 Bug 3 — Silent NA-mask divergence (wrong data, no error)

This is the most concerning: no exception, wrong values. NA tokens are kept as literal strings instead of NA when a chunk contains only `{NA-token} + {int in [2⁶³, 2⁶⁴-1]}`.

```python
import pandas as pd

OVER = "9223372036854775808"  # 2**63
with open("f3.csv", "w") as fh:
    fh.write("c0\nabc\n")
    fh.write("\n".join("nan" if i % 5 == 0 else OVER for i in range(4_000_000)))  # ~64 MB
    fh.write("\n")

par = pd.read_csv("f3.csv", low_memory=False)
with pd.option_context("mode.max_threads", 1):
    ser = pd.read_csv("f3.csv", low_memory=False)

ser["c0"].isna().sum()   # 800000  (all "nan" -> NA)
par["c0"].isna().sum()   # 200000  (600000 "nan" kept as the literal string "nan")
```

Both columns have dtype `str`, so the per-column dtype reconciliation (`_read_csv_parallel`, which compares only `dtype.kind`) sees `str == str` and concatenates without falling back.

**Mechanism.** A chunk of only `{NA-token, uint64-range int}` overflows int64 → retries uint64 → hits `uint64_conflict` (`seen_uint && seen_null`) → routed to the "leave AS IS" branch in `_convert_tokens`, which calls `_string_convert(..., na_filter=0, ...)` (`parsers.pyx` ~L1139 / ~L1147) and emits NA tokens literally. The whole-file serial read also contains `abc`, so it takes the object branch with the real `na_filter` and masks NA. This affects default NA tokens **and** custom `na_values` (list and dict), under object/`str`/pyarrow/`numpy_nullable`. It does **not** affect empty strings, bool+NA, values that overflow uint64, or `keep_default_na=False`.

**Note on the fix:** the `na_filter=0` "AS IS" emission is intentional and tested (`test_na_values_uint64`, GH-14983 asserts uint64-conflict columns are kept literal), so this can't be fixed by simply passing `na_filter` through — that reverts GH-14983. The parallel-specific regression should instead be addressed by respecting `low_memory=False` (see below). The default `low_memory=True` case can't be made byte-identical to a whole-file read without giving up parallelism, since serial `low_memory` already gives context-dependent NA here — probably a doc note.

---

### Lower-severity

- **Bug 4 — inconsistent error *type* for incompatible explicit `dtype`.** `dtype={"c": "Int64"}` on a column of mixed float/overflow-int can raise `OverflowError` from the parallel path vs `TypeError` from serial. Both fail; only the message differs. It is deterministic (the first chunk's error propagates via ordered `future.result()`), not a thread race.
- **Bug 5 — duplicated warnings from worker threads.** A converter+dtype `ParserWarning` fires once per chunk from the `ThreadPoolExecutor` workers (serial: 1, parallel: N), with a racy `stacklevel`.
- **Bug 6 — mmap unmap deferred on the error path.** When a worker raises anything other than `ParserError`/`UnicodeDecodeError`, its traceback pins the memoryview, so `mm.close()` raises `BufferError` and is suppressed; the mapping is unmapped only when the traceback is GC'd (transient address-space/FD hold). Bug 1 and Bug 2 both exercise this path.

---

### Suggested fixes

1. **Bug 1** — catch `EmptyDataError` in name inference → `return None`.
2. **`low_memory=False` gate** — `if kwds.get("low_memory") is False: return False` in `_can_parallelize_csv`. This removes the parallel-specific part of both **Bug 2** and **Bug 3** for callers who opted out of chunked inference. (Validated: they fall back and match, 78 tests pass.)
3. **Bug 2** under default `low_memory` — additionally gate `dtype_backend="pyarrow"` or fall back when a pyarrow int chunk exceeds 2⁵³.
4. **Bug 5 / Bug 6** — polish; Bug 6 is roughly a one-liner.

### Verified solid (no divergence found)

Thread/memory safety under a 250×-repeat concurrency stress (byte-identical every run; the SIMD tokenizer scan never over-reads past the mmap end); quoted embedded newlines (a boundary inside a quote always leaves a chunk mid-quote → `EOF inside string` → fallback, incl. a 50k-embedded-newline field spanning 16 chunks); the byte-offset/chunk-boundary math (1-row × 16-worker, multibyte headers, giant lines, huge preambles); `dtype="category"`, `encoding_errors`, BOM/CRLF/no-trailing-newline, thousands/decimal, uint64+NA precision, and wide/multi-column reads.

Not tested here (would need a different environment): free-threaded (no-GIL) builds, Windows/Linux specifics.

title: BUG:  `cummax` / `cummin` incorrect for pyarrow floating dtypes
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([-4.0, -3.0, -2.0, -1.0], dtype="float64[pyarrow]")
print(s.cummax())
```

### Issue Description

`Series.cummax()` / `DataFrame.cummax()` on a pyarrow floating dtype ( `float32[pyarrow]` / `float64[pyarrow]` ) silently returns a tiny sentinel (~2.2e-308, which prints as 0.0) instead of the true running maximum whenever the running max is negative (or zero/subnormal), because the underlying `pyarrow.compute.cumulative_max` call omits start, so pyarrow defaults it to the smallest positive float instead of `-inf`. The same root cause makes `cummin` return a wrong value when the running min is `+inf` 

### Expected Behavior

`cummax` should return the true running maximum (e.g. [-4, -3, -2, -1] for [-4, -3, -2, -1]), matching the numpy-backed dtype, instead of 0.0.

```python
x1 = pd.DataFrame([1, 2, 3, 4, np.nan, None], columns=["col"], dtype="float64")
select = x1.columns == "not_in_columns"

x2.loc[:, select] = pd.NA  # same with np.nan
```

New Float64 vs old float64 (note capitalization) yields different results, when sliced by empty dataframe. In the attached sample code, in both cases we slice with empty df, however the NAN assignment goes through for Float64 dtype. The float64 behaves as expected and the assignment is ignored. 

The correct behaviour of the "float64":

title: PERF: Pure Python loops when calculating validity masks and offset arrays in Interchange Protocol
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

### Problem Description
Currently, when exporting string columns via the DataFrame Interchange Protocol (`pandas/core/interchange/column.py`), pandas processes the validity mask and offset buffers using slow element-wise Python loops:

```python
# Validity Mask loop
mask = np.zeros(shape=(len(buf),), dtype=np.bool_)
for i, obj in enumerate(buf):
    mask[i] = valid if isinstance(obj, str) else invalid

# Offsets loop
for i, v in enumerate(values):
    if isinstance(v, str):
        b = v.encode(encoding="utf-8")
        ptr += len(b)
    offsets[i + 1] = ptr
```

These manual loops incur significant overhead on larger string arrays.

#### Proposed Optimization
We can vectorize these buffer constructions using Python list comprehensions and NumPy functions:

1. Construct the boolean validity mask via `[isinstance(obj, str) for obj in buf] `and direct array casting.
2. Accumulate string byte-lengths into a list and execute a single vectorized cumulative sum call (`np.cumsum`) to generate the offsets array.

#### Performance Benchmarks
Benchmarked on a string column with 100k rows (with 5% missing values):
| Operation | Old (Master) | New (Optimized) | Speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Validity Mask** | 0.188 seconds | 0.102 seconds | **1.84x** |
| **Offsets Buffer** | 0.421 seconds | 0.267 seconds | **1.57x** |

title: PERF: High overhead in stack frame warning inspections (find_stack_level)
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

### Problem Description
Whenever pandas raises a warning, it invokes `find_stack_level()` to trace the call stack and identify the calling context outside of pandas. Currently, this function walks the stack frames and calls `inspect.getfile(frame)` inside a loop:

```python
while frame:
    filename = inspect.getfile(frame)
    if filename.startswith(pkg_dir) and not filename.startswith(test_dir):
        frame = frame.f_back
        n += 1
```

For workloads that emit multiple warnings (or libraries relying heavily on pandas warnings), this function is highly inefficient because:
1. `inspect.getfile(frame)` is slow as it does lookup caching, module parsing, and absolute path validation inside the interpreter loop.
2. It repeatedly imports `pandas` and resolves `pkg_dir` and `test_dir` paths on *every* warning invocation.

### Proposed Optimization
1. Cache the `pkg_dir` and `test_dir` paths globally at the module level.
2. Retrieve the filename directly via `frame.f_code.co_filename` instead of calling `inspect.getfile(frame)`.

### Performance Benchmarks
We benchmarked 500,000 runs of the original stack inspection vs. the optimized caching and `co_filename` check on a local environment:

| Implementation | 500,000 runs | Overhead per call |
|---|---|---|
| **Original (`master`)** | 3.67 seconds | ~7.33 microseconds |
| **Optimized** | 0.19 seconds | ~0.38 microseconds |

This yields a **~19x speedup** (95% reduction in call overhead).

title: PERF: String column serialization in Interchange protocol is slow
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example


### Problem Description
Currently, when serializing string columns to a byte buffer in the DataFrame Interchange Protocol (`pandas/core/interchange/column.py`), pandas uses a slow element-wise Python loop:

```python
for obj in buf:
    if isinstance(obj, str):
        b.extend(obj.encode(encoding="utf-8"))
```

For large DataFrames ($100k+$ or $1M+$ rows), this loop is highly inefficient because:
1. It calls `.encode("utf-8")` once for every single string element inside the Python interpreter.
2. It uses `bytearray.extend()` iteratively, introducing overhead.
3. The check `isinstance(obj, str)` is run iteratively in Python.

### Proposed Optimization
We can leverage NumPy to filter nulls/invalid elements in C-space and then perform a single C-optimized join and a single vectorized `.encode()` call:

```python
# Drop null values to avoid joining None/NaN
b = "".join(buf[pd.notna(buf)]).encode(encoding="utf-8")
```

### Performance Benchmarks
We benchmarked the original loop logic vs. the optimized NumPy mask & join approach on array sizes with 5% missing values:

| Size (Strings) | Original Loop | Optimized Python | Speedup Factor |
|---|---|---|---|
| **10,000** | 0.00530s | 0.00227s | **2.34x** |
| **100,000** | 0.06940s | 0.02344s | **2.96x** |
| **1,000,000** | 0.22295s | 0.10143s | **2.20x** |

### Pandas version checks

### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

cal = np.busdaycalendar()

pd.offsets.CustomBusinessMonthBegin(calendar=cal)
pd.offsets.CustomBusinessMonthEnd(calendar=cal)
```

### Issue Description

## Description

The type signatures for `CustomBusinessMonthBegin` and `CustomBusinessMonthEnd` are missing the `calendar` and `weekmask` keyword arguments, even though they are supported at runtime and documented.

By comparison, `CustomBusinessDay` correctly exposes the `calendar` parameter in its type signature.

As a result, valid code fails type checking with mypy.

## Reproducer

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

cal = np.busdaycalendar()

pd.offsets.CustomBusinessDay(calendar=cal)          # OK
pd.offsets.CustomBusinessMonthBegin(calendar=cal)   # mypy error
pd.offsets.CustomBusinessMonthEnd(calendar=cal)     # mypy error
```

mypy reports:

```text
error: Unexpected keyword argument "calendar" for "CustomBusinessMonthBegin"  [call-arg]
error: Unexpected keyword argument "calendar" for "CustomBusinessMonthEnd"  [call-arg]
```

## `reveal_type`

```python
from pandas.tseries.offsets import (
    CustomBusinessDay,
    CustomBusinessMonthBegin,
    CustomBusinessMonthEnd,
)

reveal_type(CustomBusinessDay)
reveal_type(CustomBusinessMonthBegin)
reveal_type(CustomBusinessMonthEnd)
```

Output:

```text
Revealed type is "def (
    n: int =,
    normalize: bool =,
    holidays: list[Any] =,
    calendar: pandas.tseries.holiday.AbstractHolidayCalendar | numpy._core.multiarray.busdaycalendar =
) -> pandas._libs.tslibs.offsets.CustomBusinessDay"

Revealed type is "def (
    n: int =,
    normalize: bool =,
    offset: datetime.timedelta =,
    holidays: list[Any] | None =
) -> pandas._libs.tslibs.offsets.CustomBusinessMonthBegin"

Revealed type is "def (
    n: int =,
    normalize: bool =,
    offset: datetime.timedelta =,
    holidays: list[Any] | None =
) -> pandas._libs.tslibs.offsets.CustomBusinessMonthEnd"
```

Notably, the month offset signatures are missing both `calendar` and `weekmask`.

## Expected behavior

The type signatures for `CustomBusinessMonthBegin` and `CustomBusinessMonthEnd` should match the documented/runtime API and accept the same customization parameters as the runtime implementation, including:

- `calendar`
- `weekmask`
- `holidays`

## Environment

- mypy 2.1.0

### Documentation

The official documentation lists the `calendar` parameter:

- https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.tseries.offsets.CustomBusinessMonthBegin.html

title: BUG: `pivot_table` with `margins=True` raises KeyError when dict aggfunc doesn't cover every aggregated column
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/development/contributing_environment.html) of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "random1": [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0],
        "random2": [10, 20, 30, 40],
        "type": ["a", "a", "b", "b"],
    }
)

# aggfunc only covers "random1"; "random2" is picked up implicitly via `values`
df.pivot_table(index="type", aggfunc={"random1": "mean"}, margins=True)
```

### Issue Description

Raises:

```
KeyError: 'random2'
```

Without `margins=True`, the exact same call works fine and silently excludes `random2` from the result (since it isn't a key in the `aggfunc` dict):

```python
>>> df.pivot_table(index="type", aggfunc={"random1": "mean"})
      random1
type
a         1.5
b         3.5
```

This also reproduces when `values` is passed explicitly and includes a column not covered by the dict:

```python
df.pivot_table(index="type", values=["random1", "random2"], aggfunc={"random1": "mean"}, margins=True)
```

The root cause seems to be in `_compute_grand_margin` in `pandas/core/reshape/pivot.py`: it iterates over every column in `data[values]` and looks up `aggfunc[k]` for each one. When `aggfunc` is a dict that doesn't have a key for `k`, this will raise a `KeyError`, which propagates uncaught (only `TypeError` is currently swallowed there). I guess the fix is to skip columns not present in the dict, consistent with the non-margins aggregation path's existing (if implicit) behavior of silently dropping such columns.

I found as an incidental, separate issue while investigating and trying to fix #12210 on my own (dict `aggfunc` containing a list of functions per column + `margins=True`). However, this is a distinct root cause/code path and reproduces independently of list-vs-scalar functions.

### Expected Behavior

`margins=True` should produce the same set of columns as `margins=False` (i.e. silently drop columns the `aggfunc` dict doesn't cover), rather than raising `KeyError`.

### Installed Versions

main branch (post `84d7518bdc`)

title: BUG: `Series.to_json()` wraps `np.uint64` values ≥ `2**63` when stored in `object` dtype
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

pd.Series([np.uint64(2**63)], dtype=object).to_json()
# '{"0":-9223372036854775808}'
```

### Issue Description

**Expected Output for Reproducible Example**

```python
'{"0":9223372036854775808}'
```

**Observed Behavior**

It appears that `np.uint64` scalars stored in `object`-dtype Series are being serialized through a signed `int64` path, causing values ≥ `2**63` to wrap to negative numbers.

```python
>>> pd.Series([np.uint64(2**63)], dtype="uint64").to_json()
'{"0":9223372036854775808}'

>>> pd.Series([np.uint64(2**63)], dtype=object).to_json()
'{"0":-9223372036854775808}'
```

**Existing tests and documentation**

- `ujson.ujson_dumps` explicitly tests Python integers up to `18446744073709551615` (`2**64 - 1`) and expects exact JSON output. [[ref]](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/f7246dccfaca04609d03820636b0caedf30672fb/pandas/tests/io/json/test_ujson.py#L540)
- `DataFrame.to_json` has a test for large uint64-looking values like `13342205958987758245`, and expects them to serialize correctly. [[ref]](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/f7246dccfaca04609d03820636b0caedf30672fb/pandas/tests/io/json/test_pandas.py#L2326)
- The docs for `to_json`/`read_json` do not appear to say "ujson only encodes up to signed int64." [[read_json ref]](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/f7246dccfaca04609d03820636b0caedf30672fb/pandas/io/json/_json.py#L535) [[to_json ref]](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/f7246dccfaca04609d03820636b0caedf30672fb/pandas/io/json/_json.py#L139)

There is one internal test comment in `pandas/tests/io/json/test_ujson.py:718`:

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/f7246dccfaca04609d03820636b0caedf30672fb/pandas/tests/io/json/test_ujson.py#L712-L726

But that test is only avoiding `np.uint64.max` in a numpy-scalar roundtrip test. This suggests the object-scalar path may already have a known limitation around `np.uint64` values.

**Debugging Hints**

From debugging, it appears the object-scalar serialization path may be converting `np.uint64` values using the signed integer conversion (`NPY_INT64`) rather than the unsigned path (`NPY_UINT64`).

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/f7246dccfaca04609d03820636b0caedf30672fb/pandas/_libs/src/vendored/ujson/python/objToJSON.c#L1627-L1631


If this is confirmed as a bug, I’d be happy to help work on a fix and open a pull request.

### Expected Behavior

`Series.to_json()` should preserve the value of `np.uint64` scalars regardless of whether they are stored in a `uint64` Series or an `object` Series.

pandas==3.1.0.dev0+1194.gf7246dccfa

### Problem Description

#65812 enabled ASan and UBsan in CI, but it doesn't detect memory leaks due to `detect_leaks=0`. AFAIU, the main idea of adding ASan in CI from #52990 was to detect memory leaks. 

### Feature Description

The ASan/UBsan job needs to be updated to detect memory leaks. Unfortunately, it's not as simple as setting `detect_leaks=1` because it will contain several false positives and suppressing `libpython` will ignore real memory leaks.

From my experience, it's best to build CPython from source with `--with-address-sanitizer --without-pymalloc` and the LSan becomes a lot better: fewer false positives and simpler suppression files.

AFAIK, it's not possible to use Pixi to manage Python dependencies from a custom interpreter, so probably will have to install python dependencies via `pip` or something similar.

See #52990.

### Problem Description

import pandas as pd
s1=pd.Series([2,9], index=['a','b'])
s2=pd.Series([11,7], index=['b','a'])
s3=s1+s2
print(s3)

s4=s1>s2
print(s4)

When performing addition between two series object pandas searches for matching index in both and does the evaluation. If any one value is missing then it it gives nan.

It would be intutive if the requirement of index order is relaxed for relational operators and only matching index is checked.

title: Add type hints to public API functions
body:
## Feature Request

### Summary
Adding type hints to public API functions would significantly improve developer experience and enable better tooling support.

### Motivation
- IDEs can provide better autocomplete and inline documentation
- Static type checkers like `mypy` can catch bugs before runtime
- New contributors can understand the expected inputs/outputs faster
- Type hints serve as machine-checked documentation

### Proposed Change
Add type annotations to all public functions:

```python
# Before:
def process(data, config=None):
    ...

# After:
from typing import Optional, Dict, Any

def process(data: Dict[str, Any], config: Optional[Dict] = None) -> bool:
    ...
```

### Additional Context
This is a non-breaking change and can be done incrementally, starting with the most-used public functions.

title: BUG: pd.date_range(freq='h') produces astronomically large freq on Python 3.14, causing OverflowError
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/v3.0.4.html) of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
print(pd.__version__)   # 3.0.4
print(pd.date_range("2026-04-17 00:00", periods=24, freq="h"))
```

### Issue Description

On **pandas 3.0.4 + Python 3.14**, `pd.date_range(..., freq="h")` raises an `OverflowError` / `OutOfBoundsTimedelta`. The `freq` argument is silently reinterpreted as an astronomically large `Hours` offset (e.g. `<281467879224592 * Hours>`) instead of `<1 * Hours>`.

The same call works correctly on **pandas 3.0.3 + Python 3.14**.

### Full traceback

```
pandas/_libs/tslibs/timedeltas.pyx:2014: OverflowError

The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception:

start = Timestamp('2026-04-17 00:00:00'), end = None, periods = 24
freq = <281467879224592 * Hours>, unit = 'us'

    def generate_regular_range(...):
        ...
        try:
            td = td.as_unit(unit, round_ok=False)
        except ValueError as err:
            raise ValueError(
                f"freq={freq} is incompatible with unit={unit}. "
                "Use a lower freq or a higher unit instead."
            ) from err

pandas/core/arrays/_ranges.py:74: ValueError:
  freq=<281467879224592 * Hours> is incompatible with unit=us.
  Use a lower freq or a higher unit instead.
```

Also observed as:

```
pandas.errors.OutOfBoundsTimedelta:
  Cannot cast 11727828301024 days 16:00:00 to unit='us' without overflow.
```

### Expected Behavior

`pd.date_range("2026-04-17 00:00", periods=24, freq="h")` should return a `DatetimeIndex` of 24 hourly timestamps, as it does on pandas 3.0.3.

### Installed Versions

- pandas: **3.0.4** (regression; **3.0.3** works)
- Python: **3.14.6**
- Platform: Linux (Docker, `linux/amd64`)

Note: `freq="h"` (lowercase) is the recommended alias since pandas 2.2 (replacing the deprecated `"H"`), so this is not a deprecated-alias issue.

title: BUG: Segfault constructing pd.Timedelta on Python 3.14 (pandas 3.0.4, regression from 3.0.3)
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.
- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

In a fresh virtualenv with **only** `pandas==3.0.4` (and its required deps `numpy`, `python-dateutil`) installed on **CPython 3.14**:

```python
import pandas as pd

pd.Timedelta(days=28)   # Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault
```

Any `Timedelta` constructor crashes the interpreter at construction time — `pd.Timedelta(days=28)`, `pd.Timedelta("28 days")`, `pd.Timedelta(28, "D")`. No DataFrame/Series is involved, no threading, single-threaded `python -c`.

### Issue Description

Constructing a `pandas.Timedelta` segfaults immediately on **pandas 3.0.4 / CPython 3.14**. This is a **regression from 3.0.3** — in the same virtualenv, downgrading only `pandas` (`3.0.4` → `3.0.3`, numpy unchanged) makes the example work, and upgrading back to `3.0.4` crashes again. So `pandas` is the only changed variable.

It reproduces with numpy **2.3.3** (pandas 3.0.4's own declared minimum for Python 3.14, `numpy>=2.3.3`) and with numpy **2.4.6**, so it is not specific to a single numpy build.

With `PYTHONFAULTHANDLER=1`, the C stack shows what looks like unbounded recursion between `pandas/_libs/tslibs/timedeltas` and numpy's `_multiarray_umath`, overflowing the C stack:

```
Current thread's C stack trace (most recent call first):
  ...python... _Py_DumpStack
  /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6(+0x45330)
  numpy/_core/_multiarray_umath.cpython-314-x86_64-linux-gnu.so(+0x101f18)
  pandas/_libs/tslibs/timedeltas.cpython-314-x86_64-linux-gnu.so(+0x541ac)
  pandas/_libs/tslibs/timedeltas.cpython-314-x86_64-linux-gnu.so(+0x590ac)
  python _PyObject_MakeTpCall+0x1e7
  pandas/_libs/tslibs/timedeltas.cpython-314-x86_64-linux-gnu.so(+0x51f12)   # (deeper frames repeat the
  pandas/_libs/tslibs/timedeltas.cpython-314-x86_64-linux-gnu.so(+0x590ac)   #  timedeltas +0x590ac <-> MakeTpCall pattern)
  python _PyObject_MakeTpCall+0x1e7
  ...
```

I haven't bisected which 3.0.4 commit introduced it, but the only `_libs` source change between 3.0.3 and 3.0.4 that touches this area is the datetime C code (e.g. the `np_datetime.c` include-order change, #65591/#65609); the maintainers will know best where to look.

`pd.Timedelta(days=28)` returns `Timedelta('28 days 00:00:00')`, as it does on pandas 3.0.3.

### Pandas version checks

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

# 50 unique ISO8601 timestamp strings, repeated up to 3000 rows
base = [f"2000-01-01T0{i % 9}:00:00.000" for i in range(50)]
```

The crash requires:
- A sufficiently large series (reproduces at ~3000 rows; does **not** reproduce at ~2000), and
- Many duplicate values (the input factorizes to a small number of unique timestamps, which routes through the `map_array` / `take` fast path).

title: BUG: Segfault constructing pd.Timedelta with numpy 2.3.x/2.4.x on Python 3.14 (pandas 3.0.4)
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the latest version of pandas (3.0.4).

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
pd.Timedelta(1, unit="D")   # interpreter exits with SIGSEGV (signal 11)
```

`import pandas` succeeds; `numpy.timedelta64(1, "D")` succeeds; the **first**
`pd.Timedelta(...)` construction crashes the interpreter. No Python traceback is
produced.

### Issue Description

On Python 3.14, `pandas==3.0.4` segfaults when constructing a `Timedelta` if the
installed numpy is in the 2.3.x–2.4.x range. The crash is a hard SIGSEGV
(exit 139), single-process and fully deterministic.

The numpy `_multiarray_umath` shared object is not stripped, so the faulting
frame symbolizes exactly:

```
#0  PyUFunc_f_f (numpy/_core/_multiarray_umath.cpython-314-x86_64-linux-gnu.so + 0xd5f58)
        => mov (%rdx),%r15            # registers at fault: rdx = 0x6, rcx = 0x0
#1  pandas/_libs/tslibs/timedeltas.cpython-314-x86_64-linux-gnu.so
#2  pandas/_libs/tslibs/timedeltas.cpython-314-x86_64-linux-gnu.so
#3  slot_tp_new -> type_call -> _PyObject_MakeTpCall    # Timedelta(1, unit='D')
```

`PyUFunc_f_f` is numpy's generic float32 unary ufunc inner loop, whose signature
is `(char **args, npy_intp *dimensions, npy_intp *steps, void *func)`. At the
fault, `rdx` (the `steps` pointer) holds `0x6` and `rcx` (`func`) is `NULL`; the
loop dereferences `steps` and segfaults.

I bisected across numpy/pandas versions, each in a clean venv (Python 3.14.5),
running only the one-liner above:

| numpy  | pandas | result  |
|--------|--------|---------|
| 2.3.5  | 3.0.3  | OK      |
| 2.3.5  | 3.0.4  | SIGSEGV |
| 2.4.6  | 3.0.4  | SIGSEGV |
| 2.5.0  | 3.0.4  | OK      |

Observations (reporting only, not asserting a cause):

- pandas 3.0.3 and 3.0.4 both declare `numpy>=2.3.3; python_version >= "3.14"`.
  3.0.3 runs fine on numpy 2.3.5; 3.0.4 segfaults on the same numpy.
- 3.0.4 runs fine on numpy 2.5.0 but segfaults on numpy 2.3.5 and 2.4.6.
- Reproduced on three different x86-64 CPUs/hosts (one with AVX2, one without)
  and inside a `python3.14` Debian-bookworm container — so it does not appear to
  be CPU- or host-specific.

### Expected Behavior

`pd.Timedelta(1, unit="D")` returns a `Timedelta` (or raises a Python exception)
rather than segfaulting, for any numpy version permitted by pandas's declared
dependency metadata.

### Installed Versions

<details>

```
python : 3.14.5 (x86_64, glibc 2.42)
pandas : 3.0.4   (manylinux x86_64 wheel, PyPI)
numpy  : 2.3.5   (manylinux x86_64 wheel, PyPI)
OS     : Linux 7.0.12 (Fedora 43); also reproduced on Debian bookworm container
install: clean venv -> `pip install numpy==2.3.5 pandas==3.0.4`
```

</details>

body:
### Pandas version checks - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas. ### Reproducible Example ```python import pandas as pd value = 'http://example.com/search?q=a"b&lang=en' html = pd.DataFrame({"url": [value]}).to_html(render_links=True, escape=True) print(html) assert "http://example.com/search?q=a"b&lang=en" in html assert 'href="http://example.com/search?q=a"b&lang=en"' in html ``` ### Issue Description `DataFrame.to_html(render_links=True, escape=True)` escapes the visible cell text, but the generated `href` attribute uses the original cell value without the same HTML escaping. The relevant implementation is in `pandas/io/formats/html.py`: ```python rs = pprint_thing(s, escape_chars=esc).strip() if self.render_links and is_url(rs): rs_unescaped = pprint_thing(s, escape_chars={}).strip() start_tag += f'' ``` With the value from the example above, the visible cell text is escaped as expected, but the `href` attribute keeps the raw double quote and ampersand. The generated table therefore has different escaping behavior between the visible URL text and the generated link URL. Current generated output includes this shape: ```html http://example.com/search?q=a"b&lang=en ``` This is surprising because `escape=True` changes the visible text to `"` and `&`, while `render_links=True` keeps the raw characters in the generated `href`. ### Expected Behavior When `escape=True` and `render_links=True` are both enabled, the generated anchor should apply consistent HTML escaping to the URL value before placing it in `href`. For example, the generated output should represent the same URL value consistently in both the anchor's `href` attribute and the visible link text. ### Installed Versions
Directly visible environment information: - pandas: 3.0.3 - Python container image: python:3.13-slim
Reproduced with pandas `3.0.3`. The same `rs_unescaped` implementation is also present on the current `main` branch at `pandas/io/formats/html.py`.

body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
python 

import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series(["xbar", "bar", "foo", "xfoo"])

print("Actual:  ", s.str.match(r"^foo|bar").tolist())
print("Expected:", s.astype(object).str.match(r"^foo|bar").tolist())





Output 
Actual:   [True, True, True, False]
Expected: [False, True, True, False]
```

### Issue Description

`Series.str.match(r"^foo|bar")` on the default (PyArrow-backed) string dtype silently returns True for "xbar" (matches "bar" at position 1 instead of requiring it at position 0), because the ^ only anchors the first alternation branch.

Object dtype (and `re.match`) anchors the whole pattern at position 0 and correctly returns False, so this is a silent regression for users on pandas 3.x with PyArrow installed.

### Expected Behavior

`Series.str.match(pat)` should anchor the entire pattern at position 0 (matching Python's `re.match` and the object-dtype behavior), so `r"^foo|bar"` should only return `True` for strings that start with `"foo"` or `"bar"`.
