title: DataFrame constructed from Index or Series mutates the original object
body:
# BUG: `DataFrame` constructed from `Index` or `Series` mutates the original object

## Description

When constructing a `DataFrame` from a pandas `Index` or `Series` containing string data, any modifications made to the new `DataFrame` unexpectedly mutate the original `Index` or `Series`. This occurs even when `.copy()` is explicitly called before passing the object to the constructor — the underlying array is reused rather than being independently tracked.

This bug does **not** affect integer-backed `Index` or `Series` objects, only string (and other extension array) types.

Additionally, this can break internal invariants — displaying a `DataFrame` whose columns were modified this way has been observed to crash the IPython kernel.

## Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

# Bug with Index input
df = pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, 2], 'B': [3, 4]})
columns = pd.DataFrame(data=df.columns.copy())
columns.loc[0, 0] = 'C'
assert df.columns[0] == 'A'  # FAILS — original Index was mutated

# Bug with string Index directly
idx = pd.Index(["A", "B"])
df2 = pd.DataFrame(idx)
df2.iloc[0, 0] = "C"
print(idx)  # Index(['C', 'B'], dtype='str') — original mutated

# Bug with string Series input
ser = pd.Series(["A", "B"])
df3 = pd.DataFrame(ser)
df3.iloc[0, 0] = "C"
print(ser)  # 0    C \n 1    B — original mutated

# No bug with integer Index (works correctly)
idx_int = pd.Index([0, 1])
df4 = pd.DataFrame(idx_int)
df4.iloc[0, 0] = 100
print(idx_int)  # Index([0, 1], dtype='int64') — unchanged
```

## Expected Behavior

```python
idx = pd.Index(["A", "B"])
df = pd.DataFrame(idx)
df.iloc[0, 0] = "C"
print(idx)  # Expected: Index(['A', 'B'], dtype='str') — unchanged
```

## Actual Behavior

```python
print(idx)  # Actual: Index(['C', 'B'], dtype='str') — original was silently mutated
```

## Installed Versions

<details>

```
pandas     : 3.1.0.dev0+37.g98ffe4c45e
numpy      : 2.3.5
python     : 3.11.14
OS         : Windows 10
```

Run `pd.show_versions()` for full details.

</details>

title: BUG: DataFrame constructor from Index/Series doesn't track CoW refs properly
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, 2], 'B': [3, 4]})
columns = pd.DataFrame(data=df.columns.copy())
columns.loc[0, 0] = 'C'

assert df.columns[0] == 'A'  # fails — it's 'C'
```

### Issue Description

If you build a `DataFrame` from an `Index` or `Series` backed by an Extension Array, CoW reference tracking is missing. The result is that mutating the new `DataFrame` can silently change the original `Index` — which obviously shouldn't happen.

On top of that, we ran into IPython kernel crashes when trying to display a `DataFrame` whose columns had been modified this way, which suggests some internal block manager invariants are getting broken too.


### Expected Behavior

`df.columns` shouldn't be affected at all. CoW means either copy the data upfront or track the reference and copy on first write — neither is happening here.

### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

s1 = pd.Series([1.0, np.nan, 3.0], index=[0, 0, 1])
s2 = pd.Series([10.0, 20.0, 30.0], index=[0, 0, 1])

res = s1.combine_first(s2)
print(res)
```

### Issue Description

In this example, we have 2 Series with the same indexes. These indexes have duplicate labels and as of my understanding, reindexing on duplicate labels is not allowed. However, I get the following output on the current main branch:

```
0     1.0
0    20.0
1     3.0
dtype: float64
```

I know that this case is a special edge case so please tell me if you agree with me or not. I also have a possible solution for this issue.

### Expected Behavior

I would expect the example to raise a ValueError:

`ValueError: cannot reindex on an axis with duplicate labels`

title: BUG: consistency with R in NA handling for categoricals comparisons (with strings)
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
# Python version
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series(["a", "b", "a", pd.NA], dtype="category")
s == "a"
# s != "a" # similar
```

```r
# R version
s <- factor(c("a", "b", "a", NA))
s == "a"
# s != "a"
```

### Issue Description

Following doc, the pandas.Categorical represent a categorical variable in classic R / S-plus fashion.

However comparison to missingness (== or !=) is handled differently.

```
# python
>>> s = pd.Series(["a", "b", "a", pd.NA], dtype="category")
... s == "a"

0     True
1    False
2     True
3    False
dtype: bool

# r
> s <- factor(c("a", "b", "a", NA))
> s == "a"
[1]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE    NA
```

### Expected Behavior

In the chunk above last element of pd.Series is False, where should be pd.NA for consistency (with R and intuition/logic)

If possible, I'd suggest to make this consistent to R (both for newcomers and to avoid boilerplate code after comparison of any categorical). Otherwise I'd suggest to notice this in: 

https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/user_guide/categorical.html#differences-to-r-s-factor

Many thanks as always, best

title: Add logging support for better observability
body:
## Feature Request

### Summary
The project would benefit from structured logging to make it easier to debug issues in production.

### Motivation
Currently it can be difficult to understand what the application is doing at runtime without adding print statements. Proper logging would:

- Allow users to control verbosity with log levels (DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR)
- Make it easier to integrate with log aggregation systems
- Help diagnose issues in production without code changes

### Proposed Implementation
```python
import logging

log = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def my_function():
    log.debug("Starting my_function")
    # ... 
    log.info("my_function completed successfully")
```

### Impact
Low risk change with high value for users running this in production environments.

title: BUG: Plotting with timezone-aware and normalized `DatetimeIndex` drops tz-info
body:
### Pandas version checks - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas. ### Reproducible Example ```python from matplotlib import ( axes as maxes, pyplot as plt, dates as mdates, ) import pandas as pd # Create a figure with two subplots fig, ax = plt.subplots(nrows=2, figsize=(8, 10), sharex=False) def print_sr_line_comparison(sr, line): print(f"{sr.name}:") print(f"{sr.index.is_normalized=}", end="\n\n") print("Series:", sr, "", "Line Data:", line.get_xdata(), "", sep="\n", end="\n\n") # Create two Series with timezone-aware DatetimeIndex, one in EST and one in UTC idx_est = pd.DatetimeIndex(["2000-01-01 00:00:00-06:00", "2000-01-02 00:00:00-06:00", "2000-01-03 00:00:00-06:00"]) idx_utc = pd.DatetimeIndex(["2000-01-01 00:00:00+00:00", "2000-01-02 00:00:00+00:00", "2000-01-03 00:00:00+00:00"]) sr_est = pd.Series(range(len(idx_est)), index=idx_est, name="EST") sr_utc = pd.Series(range(len(idx_utc)), index=idx_utc, name="UTC") + 0.2 # Plot both Series on the first subplot sr_est.plot(ax=ax[0], marker="o") sr_utc.plot(ax=ax[0], marker="s") ax[0].title.set_text("Series with regularly spaced timestamps in index") # Print comparison of Series and Line data for the first subplot print("1. Figure\n") print_sr_line_comparison(sr_est, ax[0].lines[0]) print_sr_line_comparison(sr_utc, ax[0].lines[1]) print("-----------------------------------\n\n\n") # Add an additional in index non-regular datapoint to each Series sr_est.loc["2000-01-02 12:00:00-06:00"] = 1.5 sr_est.sort_index(inplace=True) sr_utc.loc["2000-01-02 12:00:00+00:00"] = 1.7 sr_utc.sort_index(inplace=True) # Plot both Series on the second subplot ax[1].title.set_text("Series with additional non-regular datapoint") sr_est.plot(ax=ax[1], marker="o") sr_utc.plot(ax=ax[1], marker="s") # Print comparison of Series and Line data for the first subplot print("2. Figure\n") print_sr_line_comparison(sr_est, ax[1].lines[0]) print_sr_line_comparison(sr_utc, ax[1].lines[1]) print("-----------------------------------\n\n\n") # Just some formatting to have similar x-axis for axes in ax: axes: maxes.Axes axes.legend() axes.xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.DayLocator(tz="UTC")) axes.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%Y-%m-%d")) axes.xaxis.set_minor_locator(mdates.HourLocator(interval=6, tz="UTC")) axes.set_xlim(pd.Timestamp("2000-01-01 00:00:00+00:00"), pd.Timestamp("2000-01-04 00:00:00+00:00")) axes.grid(True, which="major", linestyle="-", linewidth=1) axes.grid(True, which="minor", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.5) fig.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ### Issue Description While writing tests for the plotting of ExtensionArrays (#64535) I noticed that under certain circumstances a `DatetimeIndex` used for the x-axis is converted to `Period` and thereby is losing the timezone information. This seems to be only happing if the `DatetimeIndex` is normalized (i.e. a frequency `freq` can be determinated) and if the `DatetimeIndex` aligns perfectly with `Period`, e.g. time is midnight/`00:00:00` for day frequency or time is on the full hour/`xx:00:00` for hourly. As a result of the loss of timezone information different Series with same "native time", but different timezone, e.g. the Series above with `EST` respectively `UTC` timezone, are plotted at the same times (top plot), whereas in reality the datapoints should be separated by 6 hours. On the contrary Series with non-normalized `DatetimeIndex` or a not-aligned one are correctly plotted (bottom plot):
Full debug printing output of the example above ```python 1. Figure EST: sr.index.is_normalized=True Series: 2000-01-01 00:00:00-06:00 0 2000-01-02 00:00:00-06:00 1 2000-01-03 00:00:00-06:00 2 Name: EST, dtype: int64 Line Data: [Period('2000-01-01', 'D') Period('2000-01-02', 'D') Period('2000-01-03', 'D')] UTC: sr.index.is_normalized=True Series: 2000-01-01 00:00:00+00:00 0.2 2000-01-02 00:00:00+00:00 1.2 2000-01-03 00:00:00+00:00 2.2 Name: UTC, dtype: float64 Line Data: [Period('2000-01-01', 'D') Period('2000-01-02', 'D') Period('2000-01-03', 'D')] ----------------------------------- 2. Figure EST: sr.index.is_normalized=False Series: 2000-01-01 00:00:00-06:00 0.0 2000-01-02 00:00:00-06:00 1.0 2000-01-02 12:00:00-06:00 1.5 2000-01-03 00:00:00-06:00 2.0 Name: EST, dtype: float64 Line Data: [Timestamp('2000-01-01 00:00:00-0600', tz='UTC-06:00') Timestamp('2000-01-02 00:00:00-0600', tz='UTC-06:00') Timestamp('2000-01-02 12:00:00-0600', tz='UTC-06:00') Timestamp('2000-01-03 00:00:00-0600', tz='UTC-06:00')] UTC: sr.index.is_normalized=False Series: 2000-01-01 00:00:00+00:00 0.2 2000-01-02 00:00:00+00:00 1.2 2000-01-02 12:00:00+00:00 1.7 2000-01-03 00:00:00+00:00 2.2 Name: UTC, dtype: float64 Line Data: [Timestamp('2000-01-01 00:00:00+0000', tz='UTC') Timestamp('2000-01-02 00:00:00+0000', tz='UTC') Timestamp('2000-01-02 12:00:00+0000', tz='UTC') Timestamp('2000-01-03 00:00:00+0000', tz='UTC')] ```
As it can be seen in the example/graphic, adding the additional datapoint to the Series for the bottom plot, changes also the positions of all other data points as the `DatetimeIndex` is not anymore normalized. The `LineData` printed during the execution also confirms the transformation of the Series to list of `Period` objects for the first plot, while in the second plot they are transformed to a list of timezone aware `Timestamp` objects. The issue seems to come from the [`use_dynamic_x` function](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/644bf599e420c43960c26fa6225745a14f7ef156/pandas/plotting/_matplotlib/timeseries.py#L249) which determinates if `DatetimeIndex` can be converted to `Period`, but apparently failing to do so. There also was a PR recently (#63013) dealing with timezone-aware data and this function, but it has gone stale since and I do not think it would solve the issue here as the path with `index[:1].is_normalized` is not changed. I think there are also some similarities to #15754, but there were only the tick locations affected and not the data. I also do not see a common code path (anymore), but I did not dig into the issue there and if it still persists. @jbrockmendel You recently changed the comments in `use_dynamic_x` in 95405ddd7d7fefb0a05f6f271529009c201cd463 and reviewed the other PR, do you have an opinion how this should be handled? @jorisvandenbossche You commented on the other issue, maybe you also have an opinion on the topic, on the hand that one is already 7 years old, so no issue if not. While I was writing the example I also noticed the following, but not sure how they relate: 1. When I use hourly data like the following two indices then I get super weird date labels, instead of something around `2000-01-01` I got `2689-12-25` and the following days. ```python idx_est = pd.DatetimeIndex(["2000-01-01 00:00:00-06:00", "2000-01-01 01:00:00-06:00", "2000-01-01 02:00:00-06:00"]) idx_utc = pd.DatetimeIndex(["2000-01-01 00:00:00+00:00", "2000-01-01 01:00:00+00:00", "2000-01-01 02:00:00+00:00"]) ``` 2. Forcing alignment between both plots with `sharex=True`, makes the added datapoint in the bottom plot to jump from `2000-01-02 12:00:00` to `2000-01-02 00:00:00`, my first guess is the data is converted by the `PeriodConverter` set for the x-axis to the first axes (top plot) and as the frequency is `day` only mightnight values are valid. ### Expected Behavior The location of data points on the x-axis should be independent from the `DatetimeIndex` being normalized or not. It also leads very quickly to plainly wrong plots if different time zones are involved. With the data in the example I would always expect to get the horizontal displacement between the two Series of different time zone in a common plot like it is shown in the bottom plot. I am not sure if it makes sense to keep the whole `use_dynamic_x` function or if it can be reformed somehow. The biggest issue seems to be the first Series is normalized so it registers a `PeriodConverter` to that axis, but then the second Series might be a non normalized `DatetimeIndex` or has a different time zone, but is forced into the Periods defined by the first Series. ### Installed Versions
INSTALLED VERSIONS ------------------ commit : 0cdc017c38ba23a6f1759ecaf6d4bf4835fad086 python : 3.11.15 python-bits : 64 OS : Linux OS-release : 5.15.153.1-microsoft-standard-WSL2 Version : #1 SMP Fri Mar 29 23:14:13 UTC 2024 machine : x86_64 processor : x86_64 byteorder : little LC_ALL : None LANG : C.UTF-8 LOCALE : en_US.UTF-8 pandas : 3.1.0.dev0+641.g0cdc017c38 numpy : 2.4.3 dateutil : 2.9.0.post0 pip : 26.0.1 Cython : 3.2.4 sphinx : 9.0.4 IPython : 9.10.1 adbc-driver-postgresql: None adbc-driver-sqlite : None bs4 : 4.14.3 bottleneck : 1.6.0 fastparquet : 2025.12.0 fsspec : 2026.2.0 html5lib : 1.1 hypothesis : 6.151.11 gcsfs : 2026.2.0 jinja2 : 3.1.6 lxml.etree : 6.0.2 matplotlib : 3.10.8 numba : 0.65.0 numexpr : 2.14.1 odfpy : None openpyxl : 3.1.5 psycopg2 : 2.9.11 pymysql : 1.4.6 pyarrow : 23.0.1 pyiceberg : 0.11.1 pyreadstat : 1.3.3 pytest : 9.0.3 python-calamine : None pytz : 2026.1.post1 pyxlsb : 1.0.10 s3fs : 2026.2.0 scipy : 1.17.1 sqlalchemy : 2.0.49 tables : 3.11.1 tabulate : 0.10.0 xarray : 2026.2.0 xlrd : 2.0.2 xlsxwriter : 3.2.9 zstandard : 0.25.0 qtpy : None pyqt5 : None

title: BUG: `groupby(..., axis=1).plot()` throws deprecation warning with incorrect message
body:
### Pandas version checks - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas. - [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas. ### Reproducible Example ```python import numpy as np import pandas as pd datetime = ( pd.date_range("2026-01-01", freq="1D", periods=5) .append(pd.date_range("2026-01-02", freq="1D", periods=5)) .append(pd.date_range("2026-01-03", freq="1D", periods=5)) ) forecast_datetime = ( [pd.Timestamp(2026, 1, 1)] * 5 + [pd.Timestamp(2026, 1, 2)] * 5 + [pd.Timestamp(2026, 1, 3)] * 5 ) df = pd.DataFrame( { "forecast_datetime": forecast_datetime, "datetime": datetime, "value": np.random.rand(15), } ).set_index(["forecast_datetime", "datetime"]) # make single plot with one line per forecast ( df .unstack(level="forecast_datetime") ).plot() # make single plot per forecast (bad format) df.groupby(level="forecast_datetime").plot() # make single plot per forecast df.unstack(level="forecast_datetime").groupby(level="forecast_datetime", axis=1).plot() # FutureWarning: DataFrame.groupby with axis=1 is deprecated. Do `frame.T.groupby(...)` without axis instead. # following warning message gives different results due to index -> x-axis changing df.unstack(level="forecast_datetime").T.groupby(level="forecast_datetime").plot() ``` ### Issue Description Hopefully the reproducible code, messages and below plots explain the issue well enough. Plot output 1: Plot output 2 (times 3 but you get the idea with the dodgy x-axis): Plot output 3 (times 3 but x-axis is good): Plot output 4 result of following warning message: ### Expected Behavior Expected behaviour in decreasing expectedness order: 1) No warning and no deprecation for `groupby(..., axis=1).plot`. It's super useful functionality and should be preserved if possible. 2) An alternative (I've yet to figure one out) and correct warning message for `groupby(..., axis=1).plot`. 3) It seems that there might not be a way of actually making three individual plots, via `groupby`, after `groupby(..., axis=1)` future deprecation so perhaps, adding some functionality that allows users to better manage `MultiIndex` labels in plots. E.g. ```python # fixes plot output 2 df.groupby(level="forecast_datetime").plot(x_axis_level_labels=["forecast_datetime"]) ``` ```python # fixes plot output 4 df.groupby(level="forecast_datetime").plot(legend_level=["forecast_datetime"]) ``` ### Installed Versions

### Pandas version checks

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

branches = pd.DataFrame(
    data={
        "name": ["river_1", "river_2", "river_3", "river_4", "river_4-1", "pipe_51_E11", "pipe_51_E12", "pipe_52_E0"],
        "branchtype": [0,0,0,0,0,2,2,2],
        "sourceCompartmentName": [np.nan, np.nan, np.nan, np.nan, np.nan, "manhole_987_generated", "manhole_988_generated", "manhole_989_generated"],
        "targetCompartmentName": [np.nan, np.nan, np.nan, np.nan, np.nan, "manhole_988_generated",
                                  "manhole_967_generated", "manhole_990_generated"],
    },
index=[0,1,2,3,4,1002,1003,1004],
)

# print the dtype, str in pandas 2 (?) and <StringDtype(na_value=nan)> in pandas 3
# using repr since StringDtype is also printed as str otherwise
print(branches["sourceCompartmentName"].dtype.__repr__())

# does not work in pandas 3, since None is interpreted as the dype na_value
branches = branches.replace(np.nan, None)
# a useful workaround that does work
# branches = branches.replace([np.nan], [None])

print(branches.to_dict("records"))
```

### Issue Description

Context: Originally reported in https://github.com/Deltares/HYDROLIB-core/issues/1107. In our code, we would regularly initiating an object of some class (hydrolib-core BranchModel) with some parameters set to `None`. These are then considered empty/notset, consistent with many other class/method argument defaults.

This is why we need to have `None` values in our dataframes with string dtype columns (and not np.nan values). Pandas 2 supports both these values, pandas 3 implemented stringdtype to be more robust. This has a na_value argument/property, which is set to np.nan per default. This na_value cannot be set to `None` since it is considered an empty argument (which sort of makes sense to me).

However, we noticed that in pandas 3 it is actually possible to convert `np.nan` to `None`  by adding square brackets:
- `branches.replace(np.nan, None)` does not replace the np.nan values
- `branches.replace([np.nan], [None])` replaces the np.nan values with None

This is quite nice for our usecase, since we can use this as a workaround. However, this seems inconsistent and might be considered as a bug. If this is intended behaviour, that is also fine since we can then trust that the behaviour will not change in the future.

### Expected Behavior

One of these two:
- consistent behaviour between the two methods
- confirmation that this is intended and will not change in the forseeable future. Or any other suggestion to avoid the need for a workaround.

title: Potential resource leak when exception occurs during file operation
body:
## Bug Report

### Description
When an exception is raised during a file operation, the file handle may not be properly closed, leading to a resource leak.

### Steps to Reproduce
1. Open a file without using a context manager
2. Raise an exception before closing the file
3. The file handle remains open

### Expected Behavior
File handles should always be closed, even when exceptions occur.

### Suggested Fix
Use a `with` statement (context manager) to ensure the file is always closed:

```python
# Instead of:
f = open('file.txt', 'r')
data = f.read()
f.close()

# Use:
with open('file.txt', 'r') as f:
    data = f.read()
```

### Environment
- Python 3.x
- Any OS

This is a common Python pitfall that can cause issues in long-running applications.

title: [TEST]: Plotting tests fail with matplotlib 3.11.0 — color cycle returns RGB tuples instead of hex strings
body:
## BUG: Plotting tests fail with matplotlib 3.11.0 — color cycle returns RGB tuples instead of hex strings

### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import matplotlib
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
from pandas.plotting._matplotlib.style import get_standard_colors

print(f"matplotlib: {matplotlib.__version__}")  # 3.11.0
print(f"pandas: {pd.__version__}")              # 3.0.3

# Returns hex strings with mpl 3.10.x, RGB tuples with mpl 3.11.0
colors = get_standard_colors(num_colors=3)
print(colors)
# mpl 3.10.9: ['#1f77b4', '#ff7f0e', '#2ca02c']
# mpl 3.11.0: [(0.122..., 0.467..., 0.706...), (1.0, 0.498..., 0.055...), (0.173..., 0.627..., 0.173...)]

# Same issue with Line2D.get_color()
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
line, = ax.plot([1, 2, 3])
print(repr(line.get_color()))
# mpl 3.10.9: '#1f77b4'
# mpl 3.11.0: (0.12156862745098039, 0.4666666666666667, 0.7058823529411765)
plt.close()

# The colors are numerically identical:
from matplotlib.colors import to_hex
print(to_hex((0.12156862745098039, 0.4666666666666667, 0.7058823529411765)))
# '#1f77b4'
```

### Issue Description

With matplotlib 3.11.0 (released 2026-06-12), the default property cycle now returns colors as RGB tuples rather than hex strings. This causes 5 pandas plotting tests to fail:

- `tests/plotting/test_boxplot_method.py::TestDataFramePlots::test_colors_in_theme[default-expected1]`
- `tests/plotting/test_series.py::TestSeriesPlots::test_pie_series_autopct_and_fontsize`
- `tests/plotting/test_style.py::TestGetStandardColors::test_default_colors_named_undefined_prop_cycle[1-expected_name0]`
- `tests/plotting/test_style.py::TestGetStandardColors::test_default_colors_named_undefined_prop_cycle[3-expected_name1]`
- `tests/plotting/test_style.py::TestGetStandardColors::test_default_colors_named_undefined_prop_cycle[12-expected_name2]`

The upstream matplotlib change is https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/pull/29469 ("Separate property cycle handling from _process_plot_var_args"), merged in commit [`ec65514`](https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/commit/ec655143528f8e8dbc7897cc3c1e59865672c7ef) and released as part of [matplotlib 3.11.0](https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/releases/tag/v3.11.0). This refactored the internal property cycle machinery into a dedicated class. As a side effect, the default `axes.prop_cycle` rcParam now stores colors as `(R, G, B)` float tuples rather than hex strings.

The relevant matplotlib milestone: https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/milestone/96

All affected APIs are public:
- `mpl.rcParams['axes.prop_cycle']` — iterating over the cycler now yields `{'color': (R, G, B)}` dicts instead of `{'color': '#rrggbb'}` dicts
- `Line2D.get_color()` — returns whatever format was stored in the cycle, now a tuple instead of a string

The behavior change is observable through these public APIs, though matplotlib has never formally guaranteed a specific color *format* (both hex strings and RGB tuples are valid matplotlib color specifications). The pandas tests assert a specific format (hex strings) rather than comparing semantically.

### Expected Behavior

Tests should pass with matplotlib 3.11.0. The test assertions should either:

1. Normalize colors before comparison (e.g., using `matplotlib.colors.to_hex()` or `matplotlib.colors.same_color()`), or
2. Compare in a format-agnostic way that handles both hex strings and RGB tuples.

Additionally, if `get_standard_colors()` has a documented contract about its return format, it may be worth normalizing the output within that function itself so downstream consumers aren't affected by matplotlib's internal representation changes.

### Installed Versions

<details>
<summary>Versions</summary>

- Python: 3.14
- pandas: 3.0.3
- matplotlib: 3.11.0
- numpy: 2.4.6

</details>

title: BUG: missing deprecation warning about epoch timestamps in the index in to_json()
body:
When we have a datetime64 column and writing to JSON, we get a warning about the default "epoch" `date_format` being deprecated. 
However, when the datetime64 data is in the index, we don't get the warning, while we also get epoch values:

```python
>>> df = pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, 2], 'B': [pd.Timestamp("2012-01-01"), pd.Timestamp("2012-01-02")]})
>>> df.to_json()
Pandas4Warning: The default 'epoch' date format is deprecated and will be removed in a future version, please use 'iso' date format instead.
'{"A":{"0":1,"1":2},"B":{"0":1325376000000,"1":1325462400000}}'

>>> df.set_index("B").to_json()    # <-- no warning
'{"A":{"1325376000000":1,"1325462400000":2}}'
```

Both cases work fine with `date_format="iso"`:

```python
>>> df.to_json(date_format="iso")
'{"A":{"0":1,"1":2},"B":{"0":"2012-01-01T00:00:00.000","1":"2012-01-02T00:00:00.000"}}'
>>> df.set_index("B").to_json(date_format="iso")
'{"A":{"2012-01-01T00:00:00.000":1,"2012-01-02T00:00:00.000":2}}'
```

But so if we want to be able to change to `"iso"` by default in 4.0 for both cases, we also have to warn now in both cases

title: ENH: Support %N directive in strptime parsing (to_datetime / Timestamp with format=)
body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

### Problem Description

GH-29461 / PR GH-64899 added a `%N` directive to `Timestamp.strftime` and the
array-level `strftime`, formatting nanoseconds as a 9-digit zero-padded number.
The parsing side does not accept it, so `%N` output doesn't round-trip with the
same format string:

```python
>>> ts = pd.Timestamp("2020-03-14 15:32:52.192548651")
>>> fmt = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.%N"
>>> pd.to_datetime(ts.strftime(fmt), format=fmt)
ValueError: 'N' is a bad directive in format '%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.%N'
```

Note that pandas' strptime already parses nanoseconds via `%f` (it accepts 1-9
digits, an extension over the stdlib's 6), so this is about symmetry and
round-tripping rather than new capability. Suggested in
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/64899#pullrequestreview-4481273478.

### Feature Description

Accept `%N` in `format=` for `to_datetime`, `Timestamp`, and related parsing
paths, matching exactly 9 digits (vs `%f`'s 1-9). Likely just an entry next to
`"f"` in the `TimeRE` class and corresponding handling in `strptime.pyx`.

### Alternative Solutions

Keep parsing via `%f`, which already handles 9 digits — but then a format
string built for `%N` output can't be reused for parsing.

### Additional Context

`Period.strftime` has long supported `%n`/`%N` for formatting only; linux
`date` uses `%N` for nanoseconds.

# Recreate a list that is comparable to the actual dataset.
my_list = [val for group in teststrs
           for val in [group] * random.randint(100, 2*int(46000000/elements))]

large_str_series = pd.Series(my_list,name="MySeries")

ts1 = datetime.now().astimezone()

ts0=ts1

lidx = large_str_series.searchsorted("A4567", 'left')

ts0=ts1

title: BUG: to_parquet (pyarrow engine) opens the local file path twice
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import builtins
import os

import pandas as pd

# Spy on Python-level opens of the destination path.
target = "test.parquet"
opens = []
real_open = builtins.open

def spy_open(file, *args, **kwargs):
    if os.path.abspath(os.fspath(file)) == os.path.abspath(target):
        opens.append(args)
    return real_open(file, *args, **kwargs)

builtins.open = spy_open
try:
    pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3]}).to_parquet(target, engine="pyarrow")
finally:
    builtins.open = real_open

print(f"pandas opened the destination {len(opens)} time(s) at the Python level")

# Observed: 1  -> pandas opens the file itself via get_handle...
# ...but pyarrow ALSO opens the same path through its C++ layer and does the
# actual writing, so the path is opened twice per to_parquet call.

# On Linux this is also visible at the syscall level:
# strace -f -e trace=openat python -c \
#  "import pandas as pd; pd.DataFrame({'a':[1]}).to_parquet('x.parquet')" 2>&1 \
#  | grep -c 'x.parquet'
# two openat() calls for the same path
```

### Issue Description

For a local filesystem path, `to_parquet` with the pyarrow engine resolves the path through `pandas.io.common.get_handle` inside `_get_path_or_handle`, then unwraps the handle's .name back to a string and hands that string to pyarrow. pyarrow then opens  the same path a second time through its own (memory-mapped, multithreaded) C++ I/O layer, which is where the read/write actually happens. So every local-path call opens the destination/source twice.

Consequences:
- On POSIX: a wasted `open()`/`close()` syscall pair on every call (minor, but pointless).
- On filesystems that finalize a file's contents when the descriptor is closed (e.g. certain write-once / object-store backed filesystems): the empty pandas-side descriptor is closed after pyarrow has written and closed its own, so the empty one wins and the file is silently truncated to 0 bytes - data loss with no error raised.

### Expected Behavior

A local path should be opened exactly once. pandas should hand the string path directly to pyarrow (which opens it itself), without first opening it via `get_handle`. The repro above should print 0 Python-level opens of the destination, and strace should show a single `openat()` for the path.

(Non-fsspec URLs such as http(s):// still need `get_handle`, since pyarrow can't fetch those - only genuine local paths should skip it.)

### Issue Description

  Issue Description

  When two DataFrames with nullable integer dtypes and non-overlapping columns are combined using `DataFrame.add` with a `fill_value`, columns that are absent from one of the DataFrames are silently

  s2 = pd.Series([12, 22, 32], index=list("acd"), dtype="UInt16")

title: BUG: `DataFrame.to_dict(orient="index", into=...)` does not apply `into` to nested mappings
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd


class MyDict(dict):
    pass


df = pd.DataFrame(
    {"A": [1, 2], 
    "B": ["x", "y"]}
)

out = df.to_dict("index", into=MyDict)

print(out)
print(type(out))
print(type(out[0]))

assert isinstance(out, MyDict)
assert isinstance(out[0], MyDict)  # fails
```

### Issue Description

Running the code above raises an `AssertionError` like below.

```python
{0: {'A': 1, 'B': 'x'}, 1: {'A': 2, 'B': 'y'}}
<class '__main__.MyDict'>
<class 'dict'>
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
AssertionError                            Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[19], line 22
     18 print(type(out))
     19 print(type(out[0]))
     20 
     21 assert isinstance(out, MyDict)
---> 22 assert isinstance(out[0], MyDict)  # fails

AssertionError:
```

This suggests `DataFrame.to_dict(..., into=...)` applying `into` only to the outer mapping when `orient="index"`.

In the example above, the outer returned object is `MyDict`, but each nested row mapping is a plain `dict`.

I checked whether this behavior is intended, but the docstrings of both functions
```python
pandas.core.frame.DataFrame.to_dict()
pandas.core.methods.to_dict.to_dict()
```

describe the result as `dict-like`, but do not clarify whether nested mappings should also respect `into`:
```
    Parameters
    ----------
    orient : str {'dict', 'list', 'series', 'split', 'tight', 'records', 'index'}
        Determines the type of the values of the dictionary.
    ...
    - 'index' : dict like {index -> {column -> value}}
```

I also inspected the `to_dict` implementation in `pandas.core.methods.to_dict`.
I believe this behavior comes from the following three return paths in the `elif orient == "index"` branch:
- plain dict is used directly:
```python
            return into_c(
                (t[0], dict(zip(df.columns, map(maybe_box_native, t[1:]), strict=True)))
                for t in df.itertuples(name=None)
            )
```
```python
            return into_c(
                (t[0], dict(zip(columns, t[1:], strict=True)))
                for t in df.itertuples(name=None)
            )
```
- a dict comprehension is used directly, bypassing `into_c` for the nested mapping:
```python
            return into_c(
                (
                    t[0],
                    {
                        column: maybe_box_native(v)
                        if i in object_dtype_indices_as_set
                        else v
                        for i, (column, v) in enumerate(
                            zip(columns, t[1:], strict=True)
                        )
                    },
                )
                for t in df.itertuples(name=None)
            )
```

This could be fixed by using the standardized mapping constructor `into_c` for the nested row mappings as well. For example, the dict-comprehension branch could be changed to:
```python
            return into_c(
                (
                    t[0],
                    into_c(
                        (
                            column,
                            maybe_box_native(v)
                            if i in object_dtype_indices_as_set
                            else v,
                        )
                        for i, (column, v) in enumerate(
                            zip(columns, t[1:], strict=True)
                        )
                    ),
                )
                for t in df.itertuples(name=None)
            )
```


With this change, the following code passes:
```python

class MyDict(dict):
    pass


df = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "A": [1, 2],
        "B": ["x", "y"],
    }
)


out = to_dict(df, "index", into=MyDict)


print(out)
print(type(out))
print(type(out[0]))

assert isinstance(out, MyDict)
assert isinstance(out[0], MyDict)  # success
```

```
{0: {'A': 1, 'B': 'x'}, 1: {'A': 2, 'B': 'y'}}
<class '__main__.MyDict'>
<class '__main__.MyDict'>
```

I would be happy to open a pull request for this.

### Expected Behavior

Expected behavior:
```python
result = df.to_dict(orient="index", into=MyDict)

type(result)
# <class '__main__.MyDict'>

type(result[0])
# <class '__main__.MyDict'>
```

In other words, the result should be equivalent to:
```
MyDict(
    {
        0: MyDict({"A": 1, "B": "x"}),
        1: MyDict({"A": 2, "B": "y"}),
    }
)
```

title: BUG: assert_series_equal ignores check_series_type=False for ndarray subclass-backed Series on exact comparison path
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd 
import numpy as np

class OtherArray(np.ndarray):
    pass 

arr = np.array([1])

left = pd.Series(arr)
right = pd.Series(arr.view(OtherArray))

assert left.equals(right) 
pd.testing.assert_series_equal(left, right, check_series_type=False)
```

### Issue Description

`pd.testing.assert_series_equal` fails when comparing two equal `Series` objects if one is backed by a plain `np.ndarray` and the other is backed by an `np.ndarray` subclass, even when `check_series_type=False` is passed.

In the reproduction, you can observe that the two Series have the same dtype, values, index, and compare equal via `Series.equals`, but `assert_series_equal` still fails because it checks the concrete class of the internal backing arrays.

The error message is also misleading: it reports “Series classes are different”, but the classes shown are the backing array classes (`ndarray` vs `OtherArray`), not the `Series` classes.

 Full error:

```
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
AssertionError                            Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[3], line 13
     10 right = pd.Series(arr.view(OtherArray))
     12 assert left.equals(right) 
---> 13 pd.testing.assert_series_equal(left, right, check_series_type=False)

    [... skipping hidden 3 frame]

File <hidden_path>/lib/python3.13/site-packages/pandas/_testing/asserters.py:620, in raise_assert_detail(obj, message, left, right, diff, first_diff, index_values)
    617 if first_diff is not None:
    618     msg += f"\n{first_diff}"
--> 620 raise AssertionError(msg)

AssertionError: Series are different

Series classes are different
[left]:  ndarray
[right]: OtherArray
```

### Expected Behavior

The assertion should pass, since both objects are Series, their values are equal, their dtype is equal, and `check_series_type=False` indicates that concrete Series type differences should not be checked.

I suspect the right fix is for the `check_series_type` check to propogate into `assert_numpy_array_equal`

title: BUG: Incoherent dynamic dtype changes in `.map()`
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.

### Issue Description

In `a.map(b)`, when both a and b are Series and b's dtype is non-nullable, Pandas dynamically changes the output dtype if it can't match all the keys.

This behaviour changed in the nightlies vs. 3.0; however I am seeing inconsistencies which make little sense to me.

### Use case 1: Not all elements of `a.values` are in `b.index`
```python
a = pd.Series([1, 2])
b = pd.Series([10, 20], index=[2, 3])
```
output (pandas 3.0): np.float64
output (pandas 3.1 nightly): np.float64

### Use case 2: Some values of `a` are NULL
```python
a = pd.Series([1, None], dtype="Int16")
b = pd.Series([10, 20], index=[2, 1])
```
output (pandas 3.0): np.float64
output (pandas 3.1 nightly): Float64

```python
a = pd.Series([1, None], dtype="int16[pyarrow]")
b = pd.Series([10, 20], index=[2, 1])
```
output (pandas 3.0): np.float64
output (pandas 3.1 nightly): double[pyarrow]

### Use case 3: All values of `a` are NULL
```python
a = pd.Series([None, None], dtype="Int16")
b = pd.Series([10, 20], index=[2, 1])
```
output (pandas 3.0): np.float64
output (pandas 3.1 nightly): Int16

```python
a = pd.Series([None, None], dtype="int16[pyarrow]")
b = pd.Series([10, 20], index=[2, 1])
```
output (pandas 3.0): np.float64
output (pandas 3.1 nightly): double[pyarrow]


### Expected Behavior

IMHO there should be no difference in output in the three use cases.
Any of these output dtypes make sense to me:  

- `np.float64` (pandas 3.0 behaviour); on the principle that if `b.dtype` was a numpy dtype it should remain one even at the cost of loss of accuracy
- ` Int64`, or in other words the Pandas nullable equivalent of `b.dtype` (so Int8 if `b.dtype` is `np.int8`, etc.)
- `int64[pyarrow]`, or in other words the PyArrow nullable equivalent of `b.dtype`


### Installed Versions

pandas                            3.0.3
pyarrow                           24.0.0 

vs.

pandas                3.1.0.dev0+968.g384dfb2679
pyarrow               25.0.0.dev70

title: API: how to handle time zone (DST) transitions in the distant future?
body:
Historically, by using `pytz` by default for time zones, tz-aware data had wrong offsets for DST periods after 2038 (e.g. see https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/33061 and https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/28207, and documented at https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/version/3.0/user_guide/timeseries.html#working-with-time-zones (scroll down to the 5th(!) warning box), sidenote: we should update this).

The same happens if you were using `dateutil.tz` time zones, and the short summary is that pytz and dateutil are only parsing the Version 1 TZif files, those don't include a "rule" for future times, and therefore typically include transitions times extrapolated to the future, but because of 32bit are limited to dates up to 2038.

This issue was fixed by switching to `zoneinfo` by default (https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/34916) in pandas 3.0, since zoneinfo supports the newer versions of TZif files, and can use a rule-based logic for determining the offset for distant dates.

However, then after improving the performance for `zoneinfo` timezones to also use our internal fast binary search of the transition points (https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/64379) in pandas 3.0.3, this changed this behaviour again, because now we have to pre-populate our array of transition dates (to use for the binary search), and the linked PR decided to do that up to 2100 (meaning we only get correct offsets up to 2100, and not for later dates, see the example below).  
In https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/65705, I am extending that cut-off from 2100 to 2262.

While having tz-aware data so far in the future is a bit a debatable use case, having an arbitrary cut off after which it behaves differently is not ideal.

Options:

- Decide we are OK with an arbitrary cut-off if it is far enough in the future (e.g. 2262) and document this
- Populate the transition data dynamically based on the range of the input data (eg by default fill up to year 2100, but if the input data max year is 2150, we recalculate it up to that date and update the cached data)
- Use our fast-path for a "normal" range (eg up to 2100) to cover most use cases, and then for dates after that, use the `zoneinfo` python API directly as a slower fallback


--

Code illustration:

```python
import pandas as pd

import dateutil.tz
import zoneinfo
import pytz

arr = pd.to_datetime([
    "2000-01-01", "2000-07-01",
    "2036-01-01", "2036-07-01",
    "2038-01-01", "2038-07-01",
    "2100-01-01", "2100-07-01",
    "2200-01-01", "2200-07-01"
], utc=True)
```

With pytz / default in pandas < 3:

```python
>>> print(arr.tz_convert("Europe/Brussels"))   # pandas < 3
>>> print(arr.tz_convert(pytz.timezone("Europe/Brussels")))
DatetimeIndex(['2000-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2000-07-01 02:00:00+02:00',
               '2036-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2036-07-01 02:00:00+02:00',
               '2038-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2038-07-01 01:00:00+01:00',
               '2100-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2100-07-01 01:00:00+01:00',
               '2200-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2200-07-01 01:00:00+01:00'],
              dtype='datetime64[ns, Europe/Brussels]', freq=None)
```

With dateutil:

```python
>>> print(arr.tz_convert(dateutil.tz.gettz("Europe/Brussels")))
DatetimeIndex(['2000-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2000-07-01 02:00:00+02:00',
               '2036-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2036-07-01 02:00:00+02:00',
               '2038-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2038-07-01 01:00:00+01:00',
               '2100-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2100-07-01 01:00:00+01:00',
               '2200-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2200-07-01 01:00:00+01:00'],
              dtype='datetime64[us, tzfile('/usr/share/zoneinfo/Europe/Brussels')]', freq=None)
```

With zoneinfo in pandas 2.3 or 3.0.0 - 3.0.2:

```python
>>> print(arr.tz_convert("Europe/Brussels"))  # pandas >= 3.0
>>> print(arr.tz_convert(zoneinfo.ZoneInfo("Europe/Brussels")))
DatetimeIndex(['2000-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2000-07-01 02:00:00+02:00',
               '2036-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2036-07-01 02:00:00+02:00',
               '2038-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2038-07-01 02:00:00+02:00',
               '2100-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2100-07-01 02:00:00+02:00',
               '2200-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2200-07-01 02:00:00+02:00'],
              dtype='datetime64[us, Europe/Brussels]', freq=None)
```

With default zoneinfo in pandas 3.0.3:

```python
>>> print(arr.tz_convert("Europe/Brussels"))
DatetimeIndex(['2000-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2000-07-01 02:00:00+02:00',
               '2036-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2036-07-01 02:00:00+02:00',
               '2038-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2038-07-01 02:00:00+02:00',  # 2038 is now correct, but 2100 and above not
               '2100-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2100-07-01 01:00:00+02:00',
               '2200-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2200-07-01 01:00:00+02:00'],
              dtype='datetime64[us, Europe/Brussels]', freq=None)

```

title: BUG: `DataFrame.any`/`all(skipna=False)` raises ValueError instead of returning NA
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([False, None], dtype="boolean")
df = s.to_frame("a")

s.any(skipna=False)
df.any(skipna=False)
```

### Issue Description

`DataFrame.any(skipna=False)` and `DataFrame.all(skipna=False)` raise `ValueError: cannot convert float NaN to bool` on numpy-nullable columns (`boolean`, `Int*`, `UInt*`, `Float*`) whenever the reduction would propagate `pd.NA`.

The corresponding `Series.any/all(skipna=False)` reductions on the same data correctly return `pd.NA`.

`DataFrame.any(skipna=False)` and `DataFrame.all(skipna=False)` should return a `Series` with nullable boolean dtype (`boolean`) containing `pd.NA` when the corresponding `Series.any/all(skipna=False)` reduction on the same column returns `pd.NA`.

title: ENH: Add `df.corrupt()` accessor to inject random faults and typos for Data Science education
body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

In Data Science and AI education, teaching students how to clean and preprocess "dirty data" (handling missing values, detecting outliers, removing duplicates, and fixing text typos) is a critical skill. 

Currently, professors and students struggle to find realistic, messy datasets for practice. When using clean benchmark datasets (like Iris or Titanic), users have to write long, repetitive custom scripts from scratch just to artificially mess up the data for testing and educational purposes. There is no built-in, one-stop tool in Pandas to inject controlled chaos into a DataFrame.


### Feature Description

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import random
import string

@pd.api.extensions.register_dataframe_accessor("corrupt")
class CorruptAccessor:
    """
    A vectorized Pandas DataFrame accessor to inject synthetic anomalies, 
    missing values, outliers, duplicates, and smart human-like typos 
    for educational and pipeline testing purposes.
    """
    def __init__(self, pandas_obj):
        self._obj = pandas_obj

    def _resolve_count(self, param, total_elements):
        """Helper to support both exact integer counts and float percentages."""
        if isinstance(param, float) and 0.0 <= param <= 1.0:
            return int(param * total_elements)
        elif isinstance(param, (int, np.integer)):
            return int(param)
        else:
            raise TypeError("Parameters must be either an int (count) or a float between 0.0 and 1.0 (ratio).")

    def __call__(self, num_nan=0, num_outliers=0, num_duplicates=0, num_typos=0, random_state=None):
        if random_state is not None:
            np.random.seed(random_state)
            random.seed(random_state)

        # Work on a deep copy to guarantee immutability of the source dataset
        df = self._obj.copy()
        num_rows, num_cols = df.shape
        total_cells = num_rows * num_cols
        
        if num_rows == 0 or num_cols == 0:
            return df

        # --- 1. Resolve and Validate Injection Targets ---
        n_nan = self._resolve_count(num_nan, total_cells)
        if n_nan > total_cells:
            raise ValueError(f"Resolved NaNs ({n_nan}) cannot exceed total cells ({total_cells}).")

        numeric_cols = df.select_dtypes(include=[np.number]).columns
        total_numeric_cells = num_rows * len(numeric_cols)
        n_outliers = self._resolve_count(num_outliers, total_numeric_cells)
        if n_outliers > total_numeric_cells:
            raise ValueError(f"Resolved outliers ({n_outliers}) cannot exceed total numeric cells ({total_numeric_cells}).")

        n_duplicates = self._resolve_count(num_duplicates, num_rows)
        
        text_cols = df.select_dtypes(include=['object', 'string']).columns
        total_text_cells = num_rows * len(text_cols)
        n_typos = self._resolve_count(num_typos, total_text_cells)
        if n_typos > total_text_cells:
            raise ValueError(f"Resolved typos ({n_typos}) cannot exceed total text cells ({total_text_cells}).")

        # --- 2. Vectorized Fault Injection Pipelines ---

        # Pipeline A: Global Vectorized NaN Injection
        if n_nan > 0:
            flat_indices = np.random.choice(total_cells, size=n_nan, replace=False)
            nan_mask = np.zeros(total_cells, dtype=bool)
            nan_mask[flat_indices] = True
            nan_mask = nan_mask.reshape(num_rows, num_cols)
            
            for i, col in enumerate(df.columns):
                col_mask = nan_mask[:, i]
                if col_mask.any():
                    df.iloc[col_mask, i] = np.nan

        # Pipeline B: Statistically Robust Outlier Injection (Vectorized per Column)
        if n_outliers > 0 and len(numeric_cols) > 0:
            flat_num_indices = np.random.choice(total_numeric_cells, size=n_outliers, replace=False)
            outlier_mask = np.zeros(total_numeric_cells, dtype=bool).reshape(num_rows, len(numeric_cols))
            outlier_mask.ravel()[flat_num_indices] = True
            
            for i, col in enumerate(numeric_cols):
                col_mask = outlier_mask[:, i]
                if col_mask.any():
                    std_dev = df[col].std()
                    if pd.isna(std_dev) or std_dev == 0:
                        std_dev = 1.0
                    df.loc[col_mask, col] = (df.loc[col_mask, col] * 3) + (5 * std_dev)

        # Pipeline C: Vectorized Duplicate Injection
        if n_duplicates > 0:
            duplicated_rows = df.sample(n=n_duplicates, replace=True, random_state=random_state)
            df = pd.concat([df, duplicated_rows], ignore_index=True)

        # Pipeline D: Smart Realistic Text Typo Injection
        if n_typos > 0 and len(text_cols) > 0:
            flat_text_indices = np.random.choice(total_text_cells, size=n_typos, replace=False)
            typo_mask = np.zeros(total_text_cells, dtype=bool).reshape(num_rows, len(text_cols))
            typo_mask.ravel()[flat_text_indices] = True
            
            def _mutate_string(val):
                """Helper to simulate realistic human typing errors dynamically."""
                s = str(val)
                if not s or s == "nan":
                    return s
                
                # Randomly pick an error type: deletion, substitution, or insertion
                operation = random.choice(['delete', 'substitute', 'insert'])
                random_char = random.choice(string.ascii_lowercase)
                
                if len(s) <= 1:
                    return s + random_char
                
                if operation == 'delete':
                    return s[:-1]
                elif operation == 'substitute':
                    return s[:-1] + random_char
                else:  # insert
                    return s + random_char

            for i, col in enumerate(text_cols):
                col_mask = typo_mask[:, i]
                if col_mask.any():
                    # Apply the dynamic typo mutation function strictly to the masked cells
                    df.loc[col_mask, col] = df.loc[col_mask, col].apply(_mutate_string)

        return df



### Alternative Solutions

### Current Workaround / Alternative Code:

Currently, users and educators have to write verbose, loop-heavy, or non-vectorized custom functions to perturb their data cell-by-cell. A typical suboptimal workaround looks like this:

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import random

def manual_corrupt(df, num_nan=0, num_typos=0):
    df_dirty = df.copy()
    
    # 1. Non-vectorized manual loop for NaNs
    if num_nan > 0:
        for _ in range(num_nan):
            r = random.randint(0, df_dirty.shape[0] - 1)
            c = random.randint(0, df_dirty.shape[1] - 1)
            df_dirty.iat[r, c] = np.nan
            
    # 2. Slow cell-by-cell scalar string manipulation for typos
    text_cols = df_dirty.select_dtypes(include=['object', 'string']).columns
    if num_typos > 0 and len(text_cols) > 0:
        for _ in range(num_typos):
            r = random.randint(0, df_dirty.shape[0] - 1)
            col = random.choice(text_cols)
            current_val = str(df_dirty.at[r, col])
            # Naive typo injection (just drops the last character)
            if len(current_val) > 1:
                df_dirty.at[r, col] = current_val[:-1]
                
    return df_dirty


### Additional Context

This feature would significantly benefit the Data Science, Machine Learning, and AI educational ecosystem (such as university courses, bootcamps, and online interactive notebooks). 

Teaching "Data Cleaning" is notoriously hard without messy data, and creating realistic "dirty data" natively with one simple, reproducible function call (`df.corrupt(...)`) would seamlessly close the gap between pristine benchmark datasets and real-world preprocessing challenges. 

I am willing to contribute or iterate on this implementation based on core-dev feedback regarding where this best fits into the Pandas codebase.

title: ENH/API: Architectural Audit - Are other inplace=True methods bypassing CoW reference tracking?
body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

### Background
While investigating a memory corruption issue yesterday (reported in #65664  and patched in PR #65675 ), I found a structural vulnerability in how the computation engine interacts with Pandas 3.0's Copy-on-Write (CoW) architecture. 

Specifically, `df.eval("new=old", inplace=True)` was bypassing CoW protections. The `eval` engine reached into the `BlockManager`, extracted the raw data arrays, evaluated them, and handed them back. Because the data took a detour through the external computation engine, the CoW reference tracking metadata was stripped. The DataFrame assumed the returned array was unshared memory, leading to silent memory corruption when the alias was later modified.

### The Architectural Question
My patch forces an explicit `.copy()` before assignment if `inplace=True` inside `pandas.core.computation.eval`. However, this raises a much larger architectural question: **Are there other C-engine, Cython, or NumExpr-routed methods that are secretly leaking CoW tracking data when `inplace=True` is invoked?**

### Proposed Audit Targets
We know that standard `__setitem__` handles CoW perfectly. But any method that extracts raw arrays, computes externally, and attempts to write back `inplace` is at risk. I propose a systematic audit of the following `inplace=True` methods to ensure they aren't making the same tracking error:

1. **`DataFrame.query(inplace=True)`:** Since this relies on the exact same underlying `pandas.core.computation` engines (`numexpr` / `python`) as `eval`, it is the most likely candidate for a parallel vulnerability.
2. **`DataFrame.where()` & `DataFrame.mask()`:** When backed by external engines or fast-path Cython blocks.
3. **`DataFrame.fillna()` & `DataFrame.replace()`:** Specifically when operating on mixed dtypes that might force a block consolidation or split during the inplace write.
4. **`DataFrame.clip()`**

### Action Items
Rather than playing whack-a-mole with memory bugs, I suggest we:
1. Identify all `inplace=True` paths that route through `numexpr` or bypass the standard `NDFrame.__setitem__` API.
2. Implement a standardized CoW "alias corruption" test suite specifically targeting these external engine routes.
3. Determine if we need a centralized validation wrapper that explicitly checks reference counts when C-engines return data for inplace assignment.

I am happy to lead the audit on `.query()` and `.where()` to start, but wanted to bring this to the core team's attention to see if there is already a broader strategy for validating `inplace` safety under CoW. Thoughts?

### Feature Description

I propose implementing a two-phase solution to secure the CoW perimeter:

**1. A Centralized Testing Utility:**
Introduce a new test utility in `pandas/tests/copy_view/` specifically designed to test external-engine mutations. 
Pseudocode:
```python
def assert_cow_inplace_safe(df, operation_func):
    """
    Ensures that an inplace operation does not corrupt aliases 
    if it routes through an external engine.
    """
    df_copy = df.copy()
    alias = df["column_name"]
    
    # Perform inplace operation that might strip CoW tracking
    operation_func(df) 
    
    # Mutate the alias
    alias.iloc[0] = modified_value
    
    # If the original dataframe was mutated, the CoW perimeter failed.
    assert_frame_equal(df, df_copy) 
```

.........
2. A C-Engine Return Wrapper:
If the audit finds multiple leaks in .query(), .where(), etc., rather than patching them individually, we should implement a validation layer inside BlockManager.setitem_inplace (or the equivalent API) that explicitly asserts: if pd.options.mode.copy_on_write: assert result.refs is safe before mapping the C-engine memory back to the dataframe.



### **Alternative Solutions**
**Alternative 1: The "Whack-a-Mole" Approach (Status Quo)**
We do nothing structurally, and wait for users to report data corruption bugs one by one as they upgrade to Pandas 3.0. This risks user trust in the new CoW architecture.

**Alternative 2: Do nothing and wait for PDEP-8**
Since `inplace=True` is broadly slated for deprecation and removal in Pandas 4.0 (PDEP-8), we could argue that investing in `inplace` infrastructure isn't worth the time. *However*, because users will be relying on Pandas 3.x during the CoW transition period, allowing silent data corruption to exist during this window is highly dangerous. We need to secure the perimeter until `inplace` is officially removed.

### Additional Context

This architectural concern was triggered by my investigation into Issue #65664, where I successfully patched a live CoW tracking bypass in `DataFrame.eval(inplace=True)` via PR #65675.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
nums = rng.choice([-1, 1], size=10_000).astype(np.int32)
df = pd.DataFrame({"nums": nums.copy()})

title: BUG: DataFrame.melt silently corrupts data on var_name output-name collisions
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "a": [10, 20], "b": [100, 200]})
# var_name collides with the id_vars column "id"
out = df.melt(id_vars="id", var_name="id")
print(out)

output :
 
    id id  value
  0  a  a     10
  1  a  a     20
  2  b  b    100
  3  b  b    200
```

### Issue Description

`DataFrame.melt` can silently overwrite `id_vars` data with variable labels when the resolved `var_name` output column collides with an `id_var` name. Related output-name collisions, such as `var_name` colliding with `value_name` or duplicate entries in a list-like `var_name`, can also produce silently incorrect output. pandas already rejects `value_name` collisions with existing column labels, but analogous output-name validation is missing for `var_name`

### Expected Behavior

melt should raise a ValueError because the requested output column names would be duplicated:

["id", "id", "value"]

The original id_vars data should not be silently overwritten.

title: PERF: pandas.io.sql.has_table slow for ADBC driver with large database
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

We actually noticed the slowness from `pandas.read_sql`, but narrowed the problem down to its call to `has_table`. We're calling `read_sql` with a query so it will always be a miss for `has_table`.

```python
import time
import pandas.io.sql as pd_sql
from adbc_driver_snowflake.dbapi import connect

with connect("<database URI>") as conn:  # Connection to a large database
    start = time.perf_counter()
    pd_sql.has_table("foo", conn)  # Where foo does not match a table
    end = time.perf_counter()
    print(f"Took {end - start} seconds")
```

The problem sees to be in [`pandas.io.sql.ADBCDatabase.has_table`](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/pandas/io/sql.py#L2429-L2431), which calls [`self.con.adbc_get_objects()`](https://arrow.apache.org/adbc/current/python/api/adbc_driver_manager.html#adbc_driver_manager.dbapi.Connection.adbc_get_objects) without passing `depth=`. The default depth is `"all"`, which enumerates objects down to the columns. Adding `depth="tables"` speeds things up dramatically for us—from 53 seconds without `depth="tables"` down to 3 seconds with.

body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame(
    {'a': range(3), 'b': range(10, 13), 'c': range(3)}
).rename(columns={'b': 'a'})

print(df)
print(df.eval('a == 1'))
print(pd.eval('a == 1', resolvers=(df,)))
```

### Issue Description

`Dataframe.eval ` behaves differently from `pandas.eval()` when a `DataFrame` contains duplicated column names.

In the example above, the `DataFrame` has two columns named `a`. Evaluating the expression `a == 1` appears to only evaluate one of the duplicated columns (the second one in this case), and returning a `pandas.Series`

In contrast, `pd.eval( ... )` evaluates both duplicated columns and returns a `DataFrame`. 

Similar to #59950

### Expected Behavior

It would be helpful to clarify whether duplicated column names are intended to be supported in both APIs. 

Possible expected behaviors could include: 
* both methods behaving similarly
* raising an explicit exception when expressions reference duplicated names

title: ENH: Improve missing column KeyError message in DataFrame access
body:
### Feature Type

- [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

# Problem Description
Currently, when users attempt to access a column that does not exist in a DataFrame using:

df["Age"]

Pandas raises a generic error message:

KeyError: 'Age'

While technically correct, this message provides very limited context for users, especially beginners.

The current behavior does not:

explain why the error occurred,
show available columns,
help users identify possible typos,
improve debugging experience.

This can make debugging slower and more frustrating for new users working with DataFrames.

Example Reproduction
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "Name": ["Pradip", "Rahul"]
})

print(df["Age"])

Current output:

KeyError: 'Age'

# Expected Behavior

The error message should provide more contextual information.

Possible improved output:

KeyError: Column 'Age' not found in DataFrame.
Available columns: ['Name']

OR:

KeyError: Column 'Age' does not exist.
Did you mean: 'Name'?

### Feature Description

# Feature Description

Enhance the DataFrame column-access error handling mechanism to produce more descriptive and user-friendly error messages when a requested column is missing.

Potential improvements include:

  1.displaying available column names,
  2.suggesting similar column names,
  3.clarifying that the requested column does not exist,
  4.improving beginner usability.

This enhancement would improve:

  debugging experience,
  developer productivity,
  accessibility for new Pandas users.

### Alternative Solutions

# Proposed Solution

Locate the internal column access logic (likely in:

pandas/core/frame.py

)

and replace the generic:

raise KeyError(key)

with a more informative exception message.

Example:

raise KeyError(
    f"Column '{key}' not found in DataFrame. "
    f"Available columns: {list(self.columns)}"
)

### Additional Context

# Additional Context

Large DataFrames

Listing all columns may create excessively long error messages for wide DataFrames.

Possible mitigation:

truncate displayed column list,
show only first few columns.

Example:

  Available columns: ['Name', 'Marks', 'Email', ...]

body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

a = np.ma.array([1, 2, 3, 4], mask=[False, True, False, True])

# BUG: mask is ignored completely
pd.array(a)
# Output:
# <IntegerArray>
# [1, 2, 3, 4]
# Length: 4, dtype: Int64

# For comparison, pd.Series handles the mask but changes dtype to float
pd.Series(a)
# Output:
# 0 1.0
# 1 NaN
# 2 3.0
# 3 NaN
# dtype: float64
```

### Issue Description

NumPy [masked arrays](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/maskedarray.generic.html#what-is-a-masked-array) are used to define arrays with missing values, similar to pandas extension arrays. However, converting to `pd.array` currently ignores the mask completely and masked values appear as regular values.

Converting to `pd.Series` does respect the missing values, but the dtype is converted to `float` and the original dtype is not preserved in all cases.

This behavior is inconsistent with user expectations and with how `pd.Series` handles masked arrays.

The same issue occurs with string masked arrays where the mask is also ignored by `pd.array`.

### Expected Behavior

Masked values should be converted to pd.NA and the appropriate nullable dtype should be preserved, such as Int64 or string, instead of ignoring the mask or coercing to float.

>>> pd.array(a)
<IntegerArray>
[1, <NA>, 3, <NA>]
Length: 4, dtype: Int64

title: BUG: pandas.DataFrame.max fails on datetime64[ns, ...] columns with different time zones and NaT in the data
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

ONE_TZ = pd.Timestamp("2026-01-01 15:13:44.01234567", tz="Europe/Budapest")
OTHER_TZ = pd.Timestamp("2026-01-01 15:13:44.01234567", tz="Europe/Moscow")

# Example (works): different timezones, no NaT
df1 = pd.DataFrame({"time1":[ONE_TZ, ONE_TZ], "time2":[OTHER_TZ, OTHER_TZ]})
df1.max(axis=1) # Works

# Example (works): same timezone, with NaT
df2 = pd.DataFrame({"time1":[ONE_TZ, ONE_TZ], "time2":[ONE_TZ, pd.Timestamp("")]})
df2.max(axis=1) # Works

# Example (fails): different timezone, with NaT
df3 = pd.DataFrame({"time1":[ONE_TZ, ONE_TZ], "time2":[OTHER_TZ, pd.Timestamp("")]})
df3.max(axis=1) # Fails, as soon as we have a NaT
```

### Issue Description

In dataframes with datetime64 columns, max() fails with a `TypeError: '>=' not supported between instances of 'Timestamp' and 'float'` when 2 different timezones and NaT values are both present. As long as we have 1 timezone or no NaTs, everything works as expected. The default behavior of max() is skipping nans, and NaT is interpreted as such correctly with the same timezone. Once the timezone is different, it is treated as a float and the comparison fails.

It seems like during the max() operation, since timezones differ, rows are coerced into an `object` dtype. The NaT is leaking into the underlying numpy amax as a float instead of being safely skipped or masked out before the comparison occurs.

### Expected Behavior

Truly skipping NaTs as a default in max() before attempting the comparison of the remaining datetime64 values.

### Installed Versions

<details>

- Describing the meaning of the `enable` parameter

This makes the function easier to understand, reduces the likelihood of misuse, and improves maintainability for contributors.

title: BUG: `Series.values` returns inconsistent type (`ndarray` vs `MaskedArray`) depending on whether DataFrame rows are pre-sorted by groupby key
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

print(pd.__version__)

bins = np.linspace(0., 100., 101)
xc   = 0.5 * (bins[1:] + bins[:-1])

for label, x, y in [
    ("non-empty, y sorted by bin",   np.ma.array([0.1, 0.2, 0.3]), np.array([25., 50., 75.])),
    ("non-empty, y unsorted by bin", np.ma.array([0.1, 0.2, 0.3]), np.array([50., 75., 25.])),
    ("empty",                        np.ma.array([], dtype=float),  np.array([])),
]:
    df = pd.DataFrame()
    df["x"] = x
    df["y"] = y
    df = df.loc[:, ["x", "y"]]
    df.reset_index(inplace=True)
    df["bin"] = pd.cut(df["y"].values, bins=bins, labels=[str(c) for c in xc])
    for name, grp in df.groupby("bin", observed=False):
        print(f"{label}: {type(grp['x'].values).__name__}")
        break
```
prints
```
3.1.0.dev0+824.gb00d4f6710
non-empty, y sorted by bin: MaskedArray
non-empty, y unsorted by bin: ndarray
empty: MaskedArray
```

### Issue Description

When a `numpy.ma.MaskedArray` column is stored in a DataFrame and groups are iterated via `groupby(..., observed=False)`, the type returned by `Series.values` depends on whether the rows happen to be pre-sorted by the groupby key and on whether the DataFrame is empty. The same column, same dtype, same group, just different row ordering or DataFrame size, produces either `ndarray` or `MaskedArray`.

### Expected Behavior

`Series.values` should return a consistent type regardless of whether the underlying DataFrame rows are sorted, unsorted, or empty. Given the column dtype is numeric (e.g. `float64`), `ndarray` is the expected return type in all three cases.
